activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Under US law, an artwork is protected by copyright automatically the moment it is created in a fixed form; registration is voluntary, though needed before suing over a US work.
story:
The ten canvases were leaned against the fence like suspects in a lineup, and Maika walked the grass in front of them with her phone in her hand, trying to see them the way a stranger would. Nine were finished. The tenth, a small panel of the neighbor's plum tree at dusk, was half-done and had been for two weeks. Mr. Vogel had told the class in May that a portfolio needed a spine, ten pieces arguing one idea, and an artist's statement to say what the idea was. Hers was about her grandmother's hands, the way they appeared in old photographs holding tea cups, holding babies, holding the edge of a table as if steadying the world. The ninth painting had her own hand in it, holding a brush. She wasn't sure whether that was a breakthrough or a betrayal of the theme.

Hailey came through the back gate without knocking, which was the arrangement between their families, and dropped onto the overturned bucket by the birdbath. She had her laptop under her arm and an iced coffee she had clearly requisitioned from Maika's fridge, because it was the kind with the bent straw Maika's mother bought.

"You still haven't posted any of them," Hailey said. "The deadline for the scholarship is in six weeks and your entire audience is me and a birdbath."

"Everything online gets stolen." Maika said it lightly, but she had said it enough times that it had worn smooth, like a platitude she'd borrowed from somewhere and couldn't return. "I put them on the internet, some company trains a machine on them, or somebody prints them on tote bags, and there's nothing I can do."

Hailey spun the laptop toward her. "So I looked it up, actually looked it up instead of guessing like you. Under US law, your work is protected by copyright automatically the moment you create it in a fixed form. Like, the second the paint is on the canvas. It's yours."

Maika stopped walking. "Then why does everyone watermark everything?"

"Because registration is voluntary," Hailey said, reading from her notes. "You don't have to register. But you'd need to register before you could sue anybody over a US work. That's the catch. Protection is automatic, but suing isn't."

Maika sat down on the grass. The fact rearranged something in her head, quietly, the way a piece of furniture moved in a dark room. She had been imagining the internet as a place where her paintings went to become public property, stolen the instant they were seen, but the law said the opposite: they were hers at the moment of making, belonging to her the way her voice belonged to her. What she'd been afraid of wasn't losing ownership. It was something harder to name. She turned her phone over and over in the grass.

"It's not the stealing," she said finally. "It's that once it's out there, anyone can decide what my grandmother's hands mean. Some gallery person, some anonymous commenter. The statement I write becomes one voice in a hundred."

"So write a better one than theirs." Hailey said it with the insouciant certainty she brought to everything, auditions, parking, advice, and Maika both loved her for it and doubted it, because Hailey had never made anything that could be misread.

That evening, after Hailey left, Maika carried the plum tree panel to the picnic table and worked while the light failed. She thought about the fall, three years ago, when she'd painted a portrait of Eloic for his birthday and he'd posted it without asking her, and everyone at school had seen it before she was done deciding what it was. She'd been furious, though she'd told him it was fine, and only later understood that what she'd wanted was the chance to hand it over finished, chosen, given. She'd never resolved whether that was a reasonable thing to want from the world or just a childish one. The automatic copyright meant the painting had been hers even then, legally, from the first mark; it hadn't protected the thing she'd actually cared about, which had no law anywhere.

She painted until she couldn't tell blue from gray. The plum tree came out darker than she intended, the dusk heavier, and she set the brush down and looked at the ten pieces together for the first time as ten. Then she opened her phone and, on the artist's statement draft, typed one line at the top: These hands belong to the people who held me, and to no one else. She read it twice, thought it might be too much, and left it anyway. Then she photographed the plum tree panel, posted it with the other nine, no watermark, and watched the little row of images load one by one onto the screen.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: The treble clef is also called the G clef because its curl circles the second line of the staff, marking that line as the G above middle C.
story:
The choir room behind St. Brigid's was really a converted cloakroom, and Sophie had it to herself on Thursday afternoons because the organist, Mr. Asante, believed that teenagers wrote better music in rooms that smelled faintly of candle wax and old raincoats. She sat at the upright piano with a pencil behind her ear and a sheet of staff paper in front of her, sixteen empty bars waiting for the melody she had promised to bring to the youth ensemble by Sunday.

The assignment was Mr. Asante's: sixteen bars, chord changes written beneath, standard notation, no exceptions. Sophie had melodies in her head all the time, humming them in the shower, on the bus, during chemistry. What she did not have was the patience to pin them down on paper, and the difference between hearing a thing and writing it had begun to feel like the difference between weather and climate. Ronan, who played bass and sat two rows behind her in English, had offered to prognosticate her future over it. "You'll get three bars in, decide notation is oppressive, and hand him a voice memo," he said. "Historically, that's who you are."

She was proving him wrong so far. She had sketched the melody at home the night before, copying it carefully from a recording she'd made of herself humming, and today she was transferring it to staff paper to check it against the piano. The tune had come out of a walk past the church on a grey evening, and it had a shape she liked: it rose for four bars, circled back, settled. She drew the clef at the start of each line, quick loops of habit, and wrote the notes underneath.

Then she played what she had written, and it was wrong. Not ugly, exactly, but wrong, every note a third away from where her voice had put it. She played her recording, hummed along, pressed the keys again, and heard the gap. For a while she blamed the piano, then the recording, then herself. Only when she leaned down close to the page did she notice that the curl of the clef on the first line sat one line lower than the curl on the second, and that her notes had shifted with it.

She pulled the hymnal from the shelf above the piano, because Mr. Asante marked everything in hymnals and she had seen him tap the treble clef more than once during rehearsal. She found a hymn he'd annotated, compared it to her page, and saw it plainly: the curl of the clef circled the second line of the staff, marking that line as the G above middle C. Her own clef, on the first line, had quietly renamed every note she'd written. "It's called the G clef," she said aloud to the empty room, and then, feeling ridiculous, she said it again.

Dallas found her there twenty minutes later, having come to retrieve a forgotten sheet of chord charts for Sunday. He watched her redraw the clefs, loop by careful loop, watching each curl settle around the second line, and asked what she was doing. "Learning where G lives," she said, and he nodded the way people nod at musicians, as if she'd said something normal.

But here was the trouble, and she turned it over while her pencil hovered. When she played the shifted version, the wrong one, the melody had a flatness she hadn't planned, a stubborn middle-register quality that suited the words she'd half imagined for it. The corrected version climbed properly and did everything a melody was supposed to do, and she liked it less. Ronan would say she was romanticizing her own error. Mr. Asante would say that a mistake isn't a composition. Both of them were probably right, and neither had to live inside her ear.

She wrote out both versions side by side, the faithful one and the accidental one, and played them three times each, letting her hands decide by volition rather than argument. The third time through the shifted melody, she found a chord under the fifth bar that made the flatness sound deliberate, like a room chosen rather than fallen into. She pencilled it in. Somewhere in this was a distinction she couldn't quite name between music that came from her and music she'd merely found, and whether the distinction mattered, or whether the extrinsic origin of a wrong clef could disqualify a tune that had, by now, grown on her anyway. She decided it could not, and also that she wasn't sure, and wrote both feelings down as nothing, just kept going.

When Mr. Asante came through at six to lock up, she had fourteen bars done. He stood behind her for a moment, coat on, keys in hand, listening without comment. Then he leaned over the page, tapped the clef she had drawn, its curl neat around the second line, and looked at her.

"You made a copy of my clef from the hymnal," he said. "From Hymn 219."

"I did," Sophie said. "Is that cheating?"

Mr. Asante set his keys on the piano lid and pulled up the second chair.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The standard tuning note is A above middle C at 440 hertz, formalized by the International Organization for Standardization as ISO 16.
story:
Simon had commandeered the last practice room before anyone else could claim it, propping the door open with his trumpet case so the janitor would know the room was in use and not lock him out at six. He had been playing for four months, which was long enough to hit the notes and not long enough to make them sound like anything. His problem was simpler than tone, though, and it had been bothering him all week: he could not tell whether he was in tune, and everyone kept telling him to fix it by ear.

At the community center rehearsal on Tuesday, Mr. Nowak had set his phone on the stand and played a single tone through a tuner app before the band began. "A, four forty," he had said, tapping the screen. Simon had raised his hand, because he genuinely wanted to know, and asked why that note and not some other. Mr. Nowak had said only that it was the standard, written down as ISO 16 by the International Organization for Standardization, and then he had counted the band in, because forty people were waiting and a rehearsal is not a seminar. Simon had spent the rest of the evening playing slightly sharp against Kaylee's clarinet and pretending not to notice.

Now, in the practice room, he opened his own tuner app and set it to A above middle C at 440 hertz, matching the number Mr. Nowak had said. He played the note. The needle swung left, then right, then settled a hair off center. He tried again. Left. Again. He was close, but close in the way a fence is close to straight.

Kaylee appeared in the doorway with her clarinet assembled, reed in her teeth, and watched him for a minute before speaking. "You're staring at the needle like it insulted you."

"I can't get it to sit still." He played again. The needle wandered. "And half the time I can't tell if I'm flat or if the needle's just being dramatic."

Kaylee took out her phone, and after some chicanery involving a second tuner app and a tone she generated from it, they discovered that Simon's app was set to 442 hertz. He had never opened the settings; he had assumed a tuner was a tuner. He changed it back to 440, and suddenly the needle stopped arguing with him. The note he thought had been fine was, in fact, a little flat, and he pushed his tuning slide in a quarter inch and tried again. This time the needle held center, and he heard something he had not heard before, which was the app's tone and his own note beating against each other and then going still, the way two nearly identical ripples go still when they finally match.

"So it wasn't my ear," he said. "It was the machine."

"It was you trusting a machine you never checked," Kaylee said. She wanted the practice room for herself, and had for twenty minutes, but she sat down anyway on the old obsolescent piano bench in the corner, the one nobody played because half its keys didn't strike. "For the record, I tune to Natan. He's been first chair oboe since before either of us could spell oboe."

"An oboe isn't four forty," Simon said.

"It's whatever Natan's oboe is. Mr. Nowak says the tuner gets us in the neighborhood and we tune to each other from there." She shrugged. "The number's the standard. The band is the band."

Natan himself came by later, having finished his own practice, and leaned in the doorway eating sunflower seeds he was not supposed to have in the music wing. He listened to Simon play his A and said, "Sharp," and Simon adjusted, and Natan said, "Now flat," and Simon found he could hear it, a small sourness when he overshot, once he stopped watching the needle and listened instead. He was quiet for a while, working the note up and down.

"I like knowing it's a real number," Simon said finally. "A above middle C, four forty, some organization decided it. It's not a mystery. But you're tuning by feel."

"Both," Natan said, spitting a shell into his hand. "The number's the floor. The floor is useful. You still have to walk."

On Thursday, at the community center, Mr. Nowak set his phone on the stand and played the tone, and Simon matched it before the needle even settled, and then, when they moved into the chorale, he listened down the row to Natan and bent his note a fraction to meet him. Whether that fraction was right, or only comfortable, he could not have said. He held it anyway, and the chord came together around him, and Kaylee, three chairs over, glanced across and nodded once before turning back to her music.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements.
story:
Aleena's kitchen smelled like burnt popcorn and ambition. She had cleared the table, set two chairs facing each other at a stiff conversational angle, and printed a sign that said INTERVIEWS THIS WAY, which she had taped to the refrigerator as a joke, though neither of them had laughed yet.

"Sit," she said, taking the interviewer's chair and putting on reading glasses she did not need. "You're applying to be a cashier at Gristede's. I'm the manager. Don't slouch like that, you look arboreal, like a tree that gave up halfway through deciding to be a tree."

Hudson sat up. He had an actual interview on Thursday, his first, and the want behind it was specific: a bike that worked, money his mother didn't have to account for, the small externality of independence that his family absorbed every time he borrowed bus fare. He needed this job, and he needed to not blow it the way he'd blown the class presentation in April, staring at a spot three feet above everyone's heads.

"Tell me about yourself," Aleena said.

"I'm, um. Hudson. I go to school. I'm seventeen." He looked at the table, the wall, the window, the ceiling. Anywhere that wasn't her.

She lowered the glasses. "Okay. That was a hostage video. Here." She tapped her phone, waking an article she'd saved from a psych blog. "Alanna found this. In 1999, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements."

"Copy them."

"Subtly. You said it like a plan to rob a bank." She leaned forward, elbows on the table. "Like that. Watch."

He watched. She waited, and after a moment he leaned forward too, and the strange thing was that it didn't feel like copying, it felt like agreeing. "So if the manager leans back, I lean back."

"If the manager leans back, you lean back. If they cross their arms, you cross yours. Later. Not at the same time, you're not a mirror at a barbershop." She reset her posture. "Again. Tell me about yourself."

He tried again. "I'm Hudson Reyes, I'm a junior at Dunmore, and I've been babysitting my neighbor's kids for two years, which mostly means being reliable when things go wrong." Eye contact this time. She uncrossed her legs, and he let a breath pass and uncrossed his, and she smiled without seeming to know why.

"Now you're a person," she said. "Terrifying. Do it again but about weaknesses."

"I care too much."

"Absolutely not. Nobody likes that answer, it's a lie wearing a tie." They ran it four more times. Once he leaned in too fast and she said he looked like a dog that had heard the word walk. Once he held her gaze so long it became a contest, and she broke first, laughing. He was starting to think he understood it: the mirroring, the eye contact, the whole choreography. It was a way of saying I'm like you without saying it, and maybe that was slightly dishonest, and maybe everyone at every interview on earth was doing it anyway, and he decided he could live in the middle of that.

Thursday came. The manager of Gristede's was a small man named on the badge as Tom, with a coffee he never drank from. The interview went well until it didn't. Tom leaned back; Hudson leaned back. Tom folded his hands; Hudson folded his, one beat later. Tom tilted his head at the question about weekends, and Hudson tilted his, and Tom stopped, mid-tilt, and looked at him the way you look at a word you've suddenly forgotten.

"You're doing what I'm doing," Tom said.

The heat reached Hudson's face before any answer did. Every rehearsed sentence evaporated. He could deny it. He could pretend to stretch. He could claim a neck cramp, a tic, a medical externality he didn't know the word for. What he said instead was: "Yeah. A friend told me about a study. I've been practicing. I probably overdid it."

Tom set down the coffee he hadn't drunk. He was quiet long enough for the register near the door to beep at something. "My daughter does that," he said. "Copies me. Drives me crazy when I notice it." He picked up the pen and made a mark on the paper that could have meant anything. "Saturday and Sunday okay?"

Hudson rode his old bike home with the printed schedule folded in his pocket, and texted Aleena from the driveway: got the job. also got caught.

Her reply came before he'd closed the phone. "caught?? tell me everything. did he lean back when you leaned back?"

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Code-switching is moving between two languages within one conversation; it is common among fluent bilinguals and is not by itself a sign of weak skill.
story:
The debate topic was posted on Monday: five minutes, entirely in Spanish, on whether the school should switch to reusable lunch trays. Isla read it twice in the hallway outside Ms. Anderson's room, then once more, as though the word "entirely" might soften if she gave it a third chance. It did not. She had studied Spanish for four years, could conjugate the subjunctive in her sleep, and still, whenever an argument got hot, English came rushing back like a dog that had heard the treat bag.

"Five minutes," said Hadley, peering over her shoulder. Hadley was taking the opposing side and had already written two notecards, which Isla found frankly aggressive. "That's three hundred seconds of no English. Not even one sneaky little 'like.'"

"I don't say 'like' in Spanish."

"You say it in English enough for both of us."

Practice rounds began Wednesday at the picnic table behind the gym, which smelled of chlorine from the pool vents and of the fryer from the cafeteria. Isla got eleven seconds into her opening before it happened: "Los programas de reciclaje son, like, fundamentales." She stopped and put her forehead on the table. The laminate was warm and faintly sticky.

"Again," said Chantelle, who had appointed herself timekeeper and was holding a stopwatch she'd borrowed from the track coach without asking. "Also your phonetics on 'reciclaje' are tragic. It's a soft j. Like an angry whisper."

"Gracias, very perspicacious of you."

Chantelle counted the slips on her fingers through six attempts: fourteen, nine, sixteen, seven, twelve, four. "You're getting worse," she announced, delighted. "Statistically you peaked at attempt four."

What frustrated Isla wasn't the counting. It was that the slips clustered exactly where her arguments were strongest, in the sharp pivots, the "but here's the thing" moments where Spanish felt like a coat one size too small. She could describe the trays in careful, textbook sentences. She couldn't argue about them, couldn't interrupt, couldn't be quick, without English leaking through the seams. She'd started to wonder if it meant something ugly about her, some ceiling she'd hit, some proof that she was faking fluency and everyone would finally notice.

On Thursday she found Chantelle in the library, sat down, and asked the question straight out: did switching mean she was bad at this? Chantelle, whose mother spoke Tagalog on the phone every evening, whose whole kitchen ran on two languages at once, looked at her as if she'd asked whether water was wet.

"You mean the thing my mom does? That's just code-switching. Everybody fluent does it, moving between the languages in one conversation. It's not, like, a weakness thing." She turned a page of her magazine. "If anything, it's a flex."

Isla sat with that. It didn't dissolve the problem, because the rules of the debate still stood, five unbroken minutes, a constraint and not a verdict. But it reframed the thing. She wasn't leaking; she was doing what fluent brains do, and the task was to hold one channel steady for five minutes, the way a singer holds a note. That she could practice. That had a technique. That was not a flaw in her.

So she rehearsed differently. Instead of memorizing sentences, she memorized bridges, the little connective phrases that carried her across the pivots where English ambushed her: "pero considera," "además," "por el contrario." She drilled them until they were muscle. On Friday afternoon at the picnic table, with the fryer smoke drifting over and Chantelle's thumb on the stopwatch, she ran the full five minutes and slipped only twice, once on "environmental," which she gamely converted into "ambiental" mid-word so that it came out "environmental," a word belonging to no nation.

Hadley went first in the real debate and was flawless and smug about it. Then Isla stood, faced the room, and argued that reusable trays would cost more up front and less forever, that the dishwashers already existed, that the paper ones weren't recycling anyway, that a school that called itself perspicacious should act like it, and not denigrate its students by assuming they couldn't carry a tray. Five minutes. She watched the clock above Ms. Anderson's door the whole time and crossed the line with four seconds to spare.

Ms. Anderson stood to give feedback. "Excellent control, Isla. Genuinely," she said, and then, glowing, she added, "Muy bien, truly, one of the best I've seen, de verdad." She beamed at them, entirely unaware, and wrote something on her clipboard.

Chantelle leaned over from the back row and whispered, "Three seconds in."

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: Andrew Wakefield's 1998 Lancet paper claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism described just twelve children, and The Lancet fully retracted it in 2010.
story:
The bus idled outside the museum while Ms. Takahashi counted heads twice, which she always did on trips she considered risky, and Anais stood apart from the line with her phone in both hands, reading the message her uncle had sent that morning from the waiting room at the clinic. He had photographed a page from a magazine, an old article about a 1998 Lancet paper claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism, and beneath it he had typed, "Tell me what you think of this. For the baby." His wife was six months pregnant, and the baby was the reason he was at the clinic at all, arguing with a nurse about which shots were safe.

"You're going to get left," Brodie said, appearing at her shoulder with the lanyard and the laminated map that Ms. Takahashi distributed like passports. Brodie wanted the afternoon to be ordinary. He had been planning all week to reach the flight simulator on the third floor before the line formed, and anything that made Anais stop walking was a threat to that plan.

"Twelve children," Anais said. She read the sentence again. "The whole thing is about twelve children." The paper had described just twelve children, the article said, and something about the smallness of that number sat wrong with her, the way a sample of two clouds would sit wrong in a weather report.

Princess, who had been eavesdropping with the frankness she brought to everything, leaned in. "My mom used to talk about that study. She still brings it up." Princess had her own errand at the museum, a sketchbook rolled in her back pocket and a plan to sit in the hall of human origins for an hour, copying the faces of the reconstructed skulls, and she was already impatient with the detour this conversation was becoming.

Ms. Takahashi herded them through the entrance into the atrium, where a wall of screens showed a rotating Earth, and beside it a smaller auxiliary screen ran the footnote version, the credits and the data sources, in type nobody read. Anais slowed at the climate exhibit while the others moved ahead. A placard explained that the scientists did not trust any single run of the model, so they ran it hundreds of times with different starting conditions, and when the runs agreed, the agreement itself was the finding. Another placard, near the diorama of a windswept steppe where ancient horses stood frozen mid-canter, described how one fossil jawbone had suggested a whole extinct species, and how the species was only accepted after other jaws turned up in other digs, in other countries, in other hands. Nobody had believed the first jawbone on its own. Anais stood between the two exhibits with her uncle's article still open on her phone, and the architecture of the feeling became clearer to her: the problem was not that the Lancet paper had been wrong. Wrong papers happened. The problem was that twelve children had been asked to carry a weight that only hundreds of studies, checked by strangers, replicated in other labs, could hold.

She moved fast then, ahead of Brodie's objections, to the research wing where the museum kept its archive terminals, the room Princess called the boring room. Anais typed the paper's title into the database the way she had been taught, the way anyone was taught: find the paper, then find the papers that answered it. What she found stopped her. In 2010, The Lancet had fully retracted the paper. Not corrected it, not amended it. Retracted it, pulled it out of the record entirely, twelve years after it appeared, and the retraction was its own document, catalogued like a confession.

"Did you find the simulator?" Princess asked from the doorway, sketchbook already unrolled, pencil behind her ear.

"Find it yourself," Brodie said, but he had come back for Anais, and now he stood reading over her shoulder, and she watched his face change as he reached the word retracted. "It's gone? The whole thing?"

"Retracted. Fully. In 2010." She took a photo of the screen. Her uncle was still waiting in the clinic, still holding his magazine, and the weight of what to send him, and what to leave out, and whether a retraction could undo twelve years of mothers and fathers repeating a number, settled on her without resolving into anything she could say cleanly. She knew what the evidence said. She did not know what her uncle would hear.

She typed beneath the photo, "The journal took it back completely. Ask them to show you the retraction," and pressed send, and then, because Brodie was tugging her sleeve and the simulator line was forming, she pocketed the phone still buzzing in her hand and let him pull her toward the stairs.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The number of moles in a sample equals its mass in grams divided by its molar mass in grams per mole.
story:
The worksheet was due Monday, and Eric had put it off all weekend, so on Sunday afternoon he rode two buses to the science museum because admission was free for students and the chemistry hall had a lab bench where you could actually weigh things. The assignment asked him to calculate how many moles of a product would form from a given mass of reactant, and he had gotten the first two questions wrong at home, at his kitchen table, without knowing why.

Heath had come with him, ostensibly for the planetarium show, but mostly because his mother wanted him out of the house. Deacon had come because Heath had texted him a single word, "museum," and Deacon's insouciant policy was to say yes to whatever required the least planning. The three of them stood in front of an exhibit case holding brass apothecary scales from antiquity, little pans on chains, weights stamped with symbols nobody in the room could read.

"They used to weigh out everything by hand," Heath said. "No units. Just this much, whatever the old guy said."

"I need that bench," Eric said.

The bench had a digital balance, a tub of plastic chips standing in for chemicals, and a laminated card. Eric set his worksheet flat and read the question again. Given 36 grams of water as the reactant, calculate the moles. He had written 2 at home and crossed it out, then written 18, then 36, then left it blank.

Deacon leaned on the counter beside him. "You're sweating over a number."

"You're watching me sweat. Different hobby."

At the far end of the hall, Ms. Wong, the docent whose badge said her name and the word CHEMISTRY in smaller letters, was showing a younger kid how to titrate a colored vinegar sample drop by drop into a measure of base until the color changed. Eric watched her squeeze the bulb, one drop, another drop, the liquid in the flask going pale pink at the edge and then clear again. She counted drops under her breath. She didn't tell the kid an answer; she just kept the count going and let him watch for the moment the pink stayed.

Eric weighed out chips. He put chips on the balance until the display read 36, because the question said 36 grams. Then he found the periodic table printed on the bench's card and added up the molar mass of water, hydrogen and hydrogen and oxygen, and got 18 grams per mole. He sat with that for a second. At home he had stopped right there, at the 18, and guessed.

Heath leaned in. "What's the molar mass for?"

"It's grams per mole," Eric said. "One mole of this weighs 18 grams."

"So you've got 36 grams of it."

Eric divided 36 by 18 on the margin of the worksheet. Two. That was the answer he'd crossed out first. He uncrossed it with his pen, hard enough to nearly tear the paper, and then did the next question the same way: 9 grams of carbon dioxide, molar mass 44 grams per mole, 9 divided by 44, about 0.2. He checked it against the answer printed upside down at the bottom of the card, and it matched, and he sat back on the stool.

"It's just like when my dad weighs flour," he said. "The recipe says 500 grams, he weighs 500 grams, and it's the same amount of flour every time. This is the same thing, except the recipe is the mole."

"That's it? Division?"

"That's it. Mass in grams divided by molar mass in grams per mole." He said it slowly, once, the way he would say it Monday. "The whole time I thought there was a trick."

Deacon picked up one of the plastic chips and turned it over. "So what's a mole actually?"

Eric opened his mouth and then closed it. He looked at the 36 grams, and the 18, and the 2 he'd gotten, and he understood how to get the number and did not understand what the number was counting, not really, and he decided that was a Monday problem.

"Dunno yet," he said. "But I can find it now."

Ms. Wong came down the bench toward them with her squeeze bulb still in her hand. "You've got the balance the right way around," she said. "Half the people who sit there put the chips on the display side."

She tapped the edge of his worksheet, at the 9 divided by 44. "That one people always want to flip. They multiply."

"I almost did," Eric said, and covered the margin with his hand.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: DNA copying is semiconservative: each new double helix keeps one strand from the original molecule and pairs it with one newly built strand.
story:
Ella sat on the overturned crate beside the compost bins and read the same paragraph four times. The exam was Monday. Transcription, the book said, then translation, and somewhere between them the DNA had to be copied, and every sentence she read slid off her like water off the waxy leaves of Ms. Johansson's kale.

"You're doing homework in a garden," Mara said, dropping onto the crate across from her. Kristina followed with a plastic bag of cherry tomatoes she had taken from the sharing table without asking.

"Ms. Johansson said I could," Ella said. "As long as I water the cucumbers."

Kristina leaned over the book. "DNA again? I still don't get the copying part. So when a cell divides, it makes a new copy of the DNA, right? So the new cell gets the new copy and the old cell keeps the old one."

"No," Mara said. "That's not it. The copy is all new. Both strands are new. Otherwise you'd get mutations."

"That makes no sense. If it's all new, how would it be accurate? It has to keep the original somewhere."

Ella listened to them go back and forth, her finger holding her place in the paragraph. Kristina argued that the old molecule stayed intact, like a master key you never let anyone touch. Mara argued that the whole thing was rebuilt fresh each time, cell division as complete renovation. Neither of them looked at the book. Neither of them had a reason for what they believed, only the feeling that the other one was obviously wrong.

"Fine," Kristina said, turning to Ella. "You've read it. Which is it?"

"I don't know yet," Ella said. She went back to the section on replication, moving her finger along the lines. The word she found was "semiconservative," and the sentence under it said that each new double helix keeps one strand from the original molecule and pairs it with one newly built strand. She read it aloud, twice, exactly as written. "So it's half of each. Neither of you."

"It's called semiconservative," Ella said. "Half conserved, half new."

Mara frowned at the tomatoes. "Then the cell gets one old strand and one new one? Both cells do?"

"That's what it says."

"That's so weird," Kristina said. "It's like inheriting half a house and building the other half yourself." She seemed pleased with this, or at least pleased that Mara had been wrong too, and she stood up to pick more tomatoes.

Ella copied the word into her notebook and kept reading. Transcription came next: the DNA's instructions got copied into a temporary messenger, which carried them out of the nucleus to where the protein was assembled. Then translation: the messenger was read in three-letter chunks, and each chunk called for a specific amino acid, and the amino acids linked into a chain that folded into a protein. She wrote it as a sequence of arrows, DNA to messenger to protein, and then drew the copying step at the top with its split strands, one dark line for old, one light line for new.

It was Ms. Johansson, coming down the path with a watering can, who made the second half click. She stopped by the cucumbers and asked what Ella was studying, and when Ella described the arrows, Ms. Johansson said, "Like seed saving, then. You plant a row, and half of what comes up is true to the parent, and half surprises you." It wasn't exactly right, Ella thought, but something in the shape of it helped, the idea of information passing forward through a chain of copies, faithful at each step but never the original thing itself.

The evening before the exam, Ella and Mara sat on the crates again, testing each other. Mara had been vilifying the textbook all week, calling it dense and badly organized, which Ella thought was unfair; the book was dry, but it was honest, and it admitted where things were still uncertain, like which came first in early evolution, the RNA or the protein. "You just don't like that there's no one to argue with," Ella said. Mara had spent the whole semester playing iconoclast in class discussions, tearing down every model Ms. Johansson's substitute had offered, and it had become a habit, even when the model was sound.

"I like arguing," Mara admitted. "Fine. Quiz me."

Ella went through the sequence: the unwinding, the two strands, the one kept and the one built. Messenger, then the reading, then the chain of amino acids. Mara got most of it right and then, on the question of why the cell would bother keeping an old strand, said, "I don't know. Maybe as a template? You didn't ask that part."

"I don't know either," Ella said. "The book doesn't say why. It just says it happens." She wrote "why?" in the margin and underlined it once. There was a strange comfort in that, a hole she could see the edges of. She had wanted the whole process to feel like a machine, every gear accounted for, but it felt more like the garden: things that worked, and were partly understood, and went on working anyway.

On Monday she filled in the exam's long-answer question with the arrows and the strands, one dark, one light, and left the why alone. After school she walked to the garden and watered the cucumbers, then sat on the crate and read the next chapter, and Ms. Johansson came down the path with the watering can and asked how it went.

"Maybe an A," Ella said. "Ask me again in a year."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Frida Kahlo's The Two Fridas (1939) is a large, nearly square oil painting, about 173 centimetres on each side, showing two seated self-portraits side by side.
story:
Zachary had the printout of The Two Fridas taped above his desk for three days before he understood that he had been looking at it wrong. Ms. Bautista wanted a formal analysis, not the feelings-soaked paragraph he had written first, the one about pain and loneliness that had come easily and meant nothing he could defend. "You are not a connoisseur yet," she had said in class, not unkindly, holding his draft up as an example of everything a critique should avoid. "So be an analyst. Start with what you can measure."

The trouble was that he could measure almost nothing from a printout the size of a placemat. He knew the painting was big, the way he knew the ocean was wet, without any sense of what that bigness did. On Thursday night his mother asked him to set the table before she got home from her shift, and he did, and then he sat back down at the desk and pulled up his phone and called Draven, who had gone to the city museum last spring with his aunt and had actually stood in front of the real thing.

"Describe the room it was in," Zachary said.

"It was huge, first of all. Like, bigger than your garage." Draven's voice had that lazy certainty it took on when he knew something you didn't. "It's oil on canvas, and it's basically square. My aunt said about 173 centimetres on each side, and she's the kind of person who checks."

"So the two of them, the two Fridas, they fill the whole square?"

"That's the thing. You have to stand way back to get both faces at once, and even then your eyes keep jumping between them. They're sitting side by side, like they're posing together, except they're both her."

Zachary wrote 173 on a sticky note, then "nearly square," then "two seated figures side by side," and underlined nothing, because underlining was what you did to facts you already understood and he didn't yet. He tried to imagine a painting taller than his father and as wide as the hallway closet, two women in chairs occupying all of that space, and for the first time the printout seemed less like a picture and more like a floor plan shrunk down for convenience.

Marley came over Friday after cross-country practice, smelling of rain and vending-machine coffee, and sprawled on the bed while Zachary laid out his notecards. "Okay," she said, "convince me you know what you're doing, because right now those look like a hostage's ransom notes."

"Colour first," he said, pointing at the left Frida, the one in the white Victorian dress with the torn, bleeding heart. "She's in whites and blues, and she's holding the scissors. The right one is in the teal dress, the traditional one, and she's holding a little portrait of Diego. Same face, two costumes. So the colour is doing the symbolizing. The white one is exposed, cold, losing blood into the sky. The teal one holds the locket where the vein stays whole."

"And composition?"

Zachary turned the printout sideways, which was a mistake, and then back. "They're seated, side by side, and the bench they're on runs flat across the bottom, almost the whole width. Behind them the sky is stormy on the left and lighter on the right, but mostly empty, so nothing competes with the figures. If the canvas were tall and narrow they'd be stacked, one above the other, one somehow more important. Because it's square and they're side by side, they get equal room. The painting refuses to rank them."

Marley sat up, interested despite herself. "So what's your thesis? Which one wins?"

"That might be the wrong question." He had been circling this for two days, and saying it aloud felt like stepping onto ice he hadn't tested. "The European dress, the colonial dress, is the one whose heart is cut open. The Mexican dress holds the connection, the miniature of Diego, the intact vein. So you could read it as a rejection, the left Frida as the indigent one, stripped of everything, bleeding out what the other Frida keeps. But she's not smaller. She's not in a corner. The composition gives her exactly as much canvas. And it was 1939, the divorce year, so everyone wants the left one to be the discard, and maybe she is, but the painting won't say so, and I think that's on purpose."

"So you're arguing it's ambiguous," Marley said, and she made it sound like a weakness.

"I'm arguing the ambiguity is the structure. Formal analysis can get me to the square, the side-by-side, the equal space. Whether the equality is mercy or cruelty, I can't prove from the paint." He looked at the sticky note, at the 173 he had trusted Draven's aunt to verify, at the two women who had enthralled him precisely because they would not resolve. He picked up his pen, crossed out his old first sentence, and wrote a new one at the top of the page: The painting is a square, and a square has no hierarchy.

"Read that out loud," Marley said, and he did.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The notation dy/dx for a derivative comes from Gottfried Leibniz and is still standard in mathematics today.
story:
The math club met on Tuesdays in room 214, where the radiator ticked and the windows fogged near the edges by December. Evan arrived early, carrying a sheet of graph paper with a rectangle drawn on it, 30 centimeters by 20, and four small squares penciled in at the corners. His father had shown him a video about cutting the corners out of cardboard to fold an open box, and the question underneath it, the one he actually wanted answered, was which size square made the box hold the most. He had a suspicion it was the middle, some compromise, but suspicion was not mathematics.

Mr. Siddiqui had put three textbooks on the front desk, one of them open to a chapter headed "Derivatives." He did not lecture at math club; he set out problems and waited. When Evan slid his graph paper across, Mr. Siddiqui looked at it for a long moment and said, "You'll need chapter four. Borrow it, don't just look at it."

Marisa arrived with Aleksander, who was already arguing about something from lunch, some adage about practice making perfect that Aleksander insisted was a lie told to children. Marisa dropped into the seat beside Evan and read his rectangle upside down. "You want the biggest box," she said. It was not a question.

"It's a polynomial if I write it out," Evan said. He had done that part already, in the margin of his chemistry notes. If the cut squares had side x, the box's volume was x times 30 minus 2x times 20 minus 2x, which multiplied out to 400x minus 100x squared plus 4x cubed. He could graph it. He could plug in values one at a time like a person counting on his fingers. What he wanted was the moment the graph turned around, the peak, and a way to find it that wasn't guessing.

He read the chapter with his pen moving. The rule was stranger and simpler than he expected: bring the exponent down, subtract one from it. The derivative of 400x was 400. Of minus 100x squared, minus 200x. Of 4x cubed, 12x squared. Then set the whole thing equal to zero and solve. It felt like being handed a lockpick after years of prying doors with a screwdriver.

The notation bothered him, though. The book wrote the derivative as dy over dx, a stacked fraction with a d on top and a d below, and it sat there like a fraction while not behaving like any fraction he had ever met. He raised his hand before he could decide not to. "Why does it look like division if it isn't one?"

Marisa leaned over his book. She had gone ahead in the chapter last summer, at a camp, and had never needed to say so out loud; it showed in how quickly her eyes moved. "It's a leftover," she said. "It's a notation from way back." She tapped the page. "Leibniz," she said. "The notation dy/dx for a derivative comes from Leibniz, and it's still standard today." She shrugged, as if to say that mathematicians keep what works and do not much care whether it looks tidy. The notation, Evan thought, was almost vestigial, a structure from an older way of thinking that survived because it still fit the hand. People used to ascribe that survival to pure usefulness, but watching Marisa tap the page, he suspected it was closer to habit, the way his grandmother kept a landline.

He set the derivative equal to zero and factored: 12x squared minus 200x plus 400 equals zero, which shrank to 3x squared minus 50x plus 100. The quadratic formula gave him two answers, roughly 2.19 and 15.14, and the second one was absurd, a cut so large it ate the cardboard whole. The first one he checked by folding, actually folding, a scrap of paper with two-centimeter corners clipped. The box stood up on the desk between his pencil case and Marisa's elbow. She took the chapter's second problem, a farmer fencing a rectangle along a river, and worked it in silence while Aleksander narrated his own confusion across the table.

Marisa watched Evan fold and unfold his paper box twice more, measuring the base with his ruler each time as though the paper might have lied. He had the answer and still wanted to see it, which she understood; she did the same thing with proofs, reading them again after she believed them. When he finally set the box down, she pushed her own paper toward him, the fencing problem, with her answer circled. "Check mine," she said. "You're better at catching the second root being garbage." He took her page, and his pen found the factored line right away, then stopped, and he looked up at her without saying anything yet.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: During Diwali, celebrated by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists, families light small oil lamps called diyas in homes and temples to symbolize light overcoming darkness.
story:
The festival had closed off three blocks of Aungier Street, and Antoine's mother had claimed a folding table outside his uncle's shop before noon, arranging rows of tiny clay lamps with the seriousness of a general deploying troops. "Diyas," she said, pressing one into his hands. "Every home and temple will have them lit tonight." His job, before the guests and the aunties arrived, was to fill each lamp with oil, seat a wick, and set them in a straight line along the curb, because a crooked row of lights, according to his mother, brought shame upon the entire bloodline.

He wanted to be somewhere else, specifically at the stage at the far end where Jessie had texted twice about a band starting at eight. Instead he knelt on the warm pavement, oil slicking his fingers, the smell of ghee and frying onions thickening the air as food stalls fired up around them. His grandmother sat on a plastic chair supervising, telling him which neighbor's marriage to ask about and which to avoid, while somewhere behind them a speaker coughed to life with a film song so turgid with strings that even she winced and demanded it be turned down.

Clare appeared around seven, which he half expected and half dreaded, holding a paper cone of something fried. She had a way of showing up at the exact moment his two lives overlapped, and he had never decided whether he loved that about her or found it unbearable. "What are these?" she asked, crouching beside the finished row, her breath stirring the nearest flame. "Little oil lamps," Antoine said. "Diyas. They symbolize light overcoming darkness. That's the whole point of tonight, basically."

"I thought Diwali was just a Hindu thing," Clare said, and Antoine, who liked to sound like he knew things, began to pontificate on exactly that theme, something about it being the Hindu festival of lights and so on, until a man at the neighboring stall, a jeweler with silver-threaded sleeves, leaned over and cut him off without ceremony. "Hindus, yes," the man said, "but Jains too, and Sikhs, and some Buddhists as well. We all light diyas for the same reason." He held up one of his own lamps by way of evidence. Antoine felt his ears go hot, and Clare, mercifully, only raised an eyebrow.

"That's actually better," she said, standing and brushing powdered sugar off her jeans. "More people, more lamps. Light winning by numbers." She said it lightly, but it snagged on something in him, because his grandmother had said almost the same thing an hour earlier in Gujarati, that the more lamps, the harder it is for the dark to argue back. Two people who would never meet, agreeing across languages he only half commanded, and him standing between them like a badly translated sentence.

Jessie texted again. Band starting, where are you. The diyas along the curb had caught properly now, a long unbroken seam of small fires, and the guests were beginning to arrive, his uncle clasping hands and laughing too loudly, an aunt pressing a foil container of sweets on Antoine with instructions involving some cousin's engagement and an indemnity of sorts, her word for it, that he would come to the Sunday lunch and not weasel out like last time. He said yes to the lunch, and the yes cost him something, because eight o'clock was approaching and the band was not going to wait.

He looked down the street toward the stage, then at the row of flames guttering in a rising breeze, and at his grandmother, who had fallen into a low, satisfied conversation with the Jain jeweler about lamp oil of all things, two elders comparing notes on wicks while the younger generation wandered off toward noise. Maybe that was the tradition, he thought, and then stopped thinking it, because it sounded like something a person says when they are trying to make leaving feel like staying.

"Go," his grandmother said without turning around, and waved him off with the back of her hand as though shooing a pigeon. Antoine wiped his oily fingers on his jeans, took one last foil-wrapped sweet from the crate for Clare and one for Jessie, and started down the line of diyas toward the music, the little flames bending all together in the wind behind him like they were leaning in to watch him go.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Most news articles use the 'inverted pyramid': the most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story.
story:
The festival had taken over the park in long rows of white tents, and Zoey had agreed to spend two hours at the Portuguese-language booth before she understood what those hours would require. Ms. Brennan, who taught her world history and ran the school's heritage clubs, had handed her a folded newspaper that morning: a short article about a library in Lisbon reopening after a flood. Zoey's grandmother had spoken Portuguese around the house until Zoey was six, and after that it had gone quiet, and this was the whole reason she had said yes. She wanted it back, or some piece of it, though she could not have said which piece.

"You have to read it out loud at four," Ms. Brennan said, straightening a stack of flyers. "Then summarize it for whoever's listening. In Portuguese, then again in English. Ten minutes, that's all." She was already moving toward the food stalls, so Zoey sat down at the small table with the newspaper and began where anyone begins, at the beginning, except that she stalled on the second word and flipped, out of a kind of despair, to the end.

The last paragraph was dense with words she didn't know. She worked at it for twenty minutes, digging meanings out of a dictionary app while the smell of grilled sardines drifted over the table, and she had assembled something like a sentence about restoration funding when Simeon appeared beside her with a paper plate of pastéis de nata. "How's the homework going?"

"Terrible." She pointed at the final paragraph. "This part is impossible. Something about municipal budgets, I think."

Simeon, who had actually grown up in the language, pulled a chair around and squinted at the page. "Why are you doing the last paragraph first?"

"Because if I finish the hard part, the rest will be easy."

He took a pastry and broke it in half without offering her any, which was how she knew he was thinking. "Ms. Brennan calls it the inverted pyramid," he said. "Most news articles work that way. The most important facts come first, and the less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story." He tapped the top of the page. "You've been decoding the budget numbers. The flood is up here."

Zoey read the first paragraph again and found, to her annoyance, that she could. The opening gave her the library, the flood, the reopening, even a rough when, in sentences built to be understood by a reader in a hurry. The end was where the article stashed the money, the committee, the details a tired reader could skip. She had spent twenty minutes excavating the least important paragraph in the piece, and now, with the core already in hand, she could interpolate the rest, filling the gaps between words she knew with what the first lines had told her to expect. "I had it backwards," she said.

At four o'clock a small crowd had gathered, maybe fifteen people, some waiting for the dance troupe that would follow. Tamara sat cross-legged at the edge of the audience, mouthing good luck. Zoey stood, held the newspaper like a shield, and read the opening paragraph aloud, her accent rough, her grandmother's vowels surfacing in places she didn't expect, like furniture found under a dust sheet. Then she set the paper down and summarized: a library had flooded, had closed, had reopened with its collection saved. A woman in the front row, older, with silver threads in her braid, nodded slowly, and when Zoey finished, the woman said something quiet in Portuguese that Zoey caught only half of, something about patrimony, and the room around her went soft with applause that had more kindness than judgment in it.

Afterward Tamara dragged her toward the food stalls, but a man from a community aid society caught her first, pressing a flyer into her hand about volunteers reading to children at a shelter downtown, children the flyer called indigent, a word Zoey had only ever met in novels. He asked, in careful English, whether she might come on Saturdays. She said she would think about it, and she meant it, though she did not know yet whether her Portuguese was a thing she had inherited or a thing she was borrowing, whether ten recovered words and one shaky summary counted as having the language back at all.

She folded the flyer into her pocket and found Simeon at the pastry table, and she took half his second pastel de nata without asking, which she felt was fair. "Same time next year?" he said.

"Next year I'm starting with the first paragraph."

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: An 'I-message', popularized by psychologist Thomas Gordon, states the speaker's own concern, such as 'I'm worried we'll miss the deadline', instead of accusing the listener with 'you' language.
story:
John had been volunteering at the community resource office since September, filing intake forms and answering the phone in the voice Ms. Haile had coached him into, the one that sounded like a person who had his life arranged. The trouble was Nash, who had signed on in October and now left an hour early almost every shift, leaving the Monday report half-finished on the shared desk.

The deadline was real. Ms. Haile had taped a note above the copier: the county grant summary had to go out Friday by four, and it needed a cover letter signed by the volunteer team. John had agreed to write the draft, mostly because he wanted the writing practice, and now the draft depended on numbers Nash had collected on Wednesday, a Wednesday Nash had left at three.

He sat at the desk Thursday after school and opened a blank document. He typed, "Nash, you keep ditching your shifts," and then deleted it, because he could already hear how it would land. He typed instead, "Nash, your attendance has been inconsistent," which was more professional and somehow colder. The cursor blinked. Everything he wrote sounded either like an accusation or like nothing at all, some equivocal sentence that could be read two ways and would therefore be read the worst way.

He got up to look for the volunteer handbook, which Ms. Haile kept on a shelf behind the paper sorter, and found instead a laminated page, faded at the corners, tucked inside a binder labeled Conflict Resolution. It was from some old training, and partway down, under a heading about ownership of feelings, it described the I-message, popularized by a psychologist named Thomas Gordon: you state your own concern, the page said, like "I'm worried we'll miss the deadline," instead of accusing the listener with "you" language. John read it twice. It wasn't a trick for winning an argument; it was a way of telling the truth without handing the other person a weapon.

He went back to the desk and wrote:

"Nash, I'm worried we'll miss the Friday four o'clock deadline for the grant summary if the Wednesday numbers aren't in by tomorrow morning. I can build the tables if you can get me the counts tonight. If something's going on with your schedule, tell me and I'll cover it, but I need to know before noon."

He read it aloud in a mutter, checking the tone the way Ms. Haial had taught him to check the phone voice. It still felt strange, like writing a letter instead of talking to a person three feet away, though Nash was at home and the office was empty and this was the professional channel, so maybe a letter was what it was.

At ten the next morning Nash showed up with a flash drive and an expression that hadn't ionized into anything John could read yet, halfway between apologetic and annoyed. "Got your email," Nash said. "Very formal." He set the drive on the desk. "My mom's got a thing on Wednesdays. I should've said." John said that was all he'd needed to know, and Nash shrugged, and that was as close as the morning came to an apology in either direction. They built the tables together in an hour, and the letter went out at 3:41, signed by both of them, and John noticed that Nash's signature was cramped into the space like he was trying to take up less of it.

Afterward Ms. Haile read the cover letter at her desk and said it was the cleanest thing the office had sent out all year, and John didn't tell her it had nearly been a fight. He understood that he had gained something, a sentence structure that worked, and paid something too, because the formality that made the email land had also put a thin pane of glass between him and Nash, and neither of them had broken it. On his way out he checked the Wednesday schedule for next week and saw Nash's name still on it, in pen, uncorrected.

"See you Monday," Nash called from the bus stop across the street.

John raised a hand and kept walking, the laminated page folded in his back pocket.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Two Fridas, one Frida wears a white European-style Victorian dress and the other wears a traditional Tehuana dress, a contrast often read as her mixed European and Mexican heritage.
story:
Charlie had never argued about a painting before, and she discovered she liked it more than she had expected to, which was itself a little alarming. The community art studio on Halstead Street smelled of turpentine and burnt coffee, and on the third Tuesday of the summer critique workshop, Ms. Hamdan propped a print of The Two Fridas on the rickety easel by the window and said only, "Tell me what you see."

Breanna went first, as she always did, pointing at the Frida on the left in the white dress with the lace at the throat. "That one's the real one," she said. "The other one's a costume." Mary shook her head so fast her earrings swung. "No way. The one in the Tehuana dress is real. That's her actual heritage, not some colonial hand-me-down." The Tehuana dress, Charlie noted, the words landing in her notebook alongside her sketchy copy of the double self-portrait, hearts stitched together by a single thin artery.

"You're both doing it wrong," Ms. Hamdan said, before the argument could escalate. "Formal analysis. Colour, composition, symbolism. Start there and stay there until it stops working." She said it in her dry, level way, the way that made even the irascible old man who painted landscapes in the corner go quiet. Charlie raised her hand before she knew why.

"Which Frida is the real one, though," Breanna said, not a question, a demand, and Charlie felt the whole small room tilt toward her, waiting, because she was the one who had signed up for the workshop after failing the art history unit in the spring, the one who had something to prove.

"I don't think that's the right question," Charlie said, and immediately regretted the prissiness of it, so she went to the print instead of standing there. She touched the wall beside it, the way Ms. Hamdan sometimes did. "Look at the composition. They're the same size. Same face, almost. They're holding hands. The European one, the white Victorian dress, she's holding the little portrait, and the scissors, and her heart's cut open. The Tehuana one, her heart's whole." She heard herself say both words, European and Tehuana, and hoped she was saying them right, and Mary gave a small nod that suggested she was.

Breanna folded her arms. "So you're saying they're both real."

"I'm saying the painting isn't asking us to pick." Charlie was thinking of her own mother, who spoke Spanish at her mother's grave and English everywhere else, who never seemed to be performing and never seemed to be whole, and Charlie could not put that into the sentence she was building. "It's a self-portrait. There's one title, not two. But I don't know if that means they're both real or if the painting is about the question. I genuinely don't know."

"Good," said Ms. Hamdan, which startled everyone. "That's the first honest sentence tonight." She made them go on: the stormy sky behind both women, flat and lilac-grey, offering no horizon; the blood on the white dress trailing toward the hem where it might drip; the way the composition sat low in the frame so both figures seemed to float or to be displayed, Charlie couldn't decide which, and said so, and Ms. Hamdan wrote that on the board too, under a heading that read THINGS THAT STAY UNCERTAIN.

Afterward, while the others rinsed brushes, Charlie stayed by the easel. Ms. Hamdan was stacking chairs and did not look over, but she said, "Your erudition is thin, Charlie. You don't know the vocabulary yet. That's fine. You noticed the artery. Most people look at the hearts." Charlie copied the print's details into her notebook one more time, the white dress and the Tehuana dress side by side, the joined hands, and under her sketch she wrote a question mark, then, to forestall her own habit of pretending certainty, left it there.

Breanna appeared beside her with her jacket half on. "I still think the white one's how the world saw her," Breanna said, "and the other one's how she saw herself."

"Maybe," Charlie said. "Or maybe the white dress is the one she put on for Europe and the Tehuana dress is the one she put on for Mexico, and the real Frida is the one holding both hands." She heard how unsure it came out and decided not to fix it. Mary, waiting at the door, called that she was getting bubble tea and would they hurry up, and Charlie zipped her notebook into her bag, print image still burning behind her eyes, and followed them out into the orange evening street.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches

fact: Frozen food can be thawed safely in the refrigerator, in cold water or in the microwave, but not by leaving it out on the counter.
story:
Mr. Francis announced the project on a Tuesday, and Seth, who had never once planned anything further ahead than lunch, decided immediately that he was a planner by nature. Each student would map a week of meals, buy the ingredients with a ten-dollar limit per day, cook everything in batches on Friday, and eat the results on Monday. Seth considered this trivial. He told Yann it was trivial twice, once while Yann was weighing flour and once later, when Yann had stopped listening.

The planning sheet defeated him by Wednesday. He had budgeted for chicken on four consecutive nights because chicken was on sale, which struck him as shrewd rather than monotonous, and he had forgotten vegetables entirely until Edward pointed at the empty column and asked if Seth intended to live like a wolf. Seth revised. He wrote down lentils, then crossed out lentils, then wrote them again in smaller handwriting, as though they would take up less room that way. His final plan was, he informed the class, "ascetic in places, but with moments of real pleasure," and Mr. Francis said, "Interesting word," in a tone Seth chose to interpret as admiration.

The shopping trip went to Edward's mother, who drove them to the store and waited in the car with a paperback. Seth walked the aisls with his list folded into quarters. He bought the chicken, a bag of carrots, two cans of tomatoes, rice, and one bar of expensive chocolate that he classified under "contingencies." Edward, beside him, put the chocolate back on the shelf. Seth took it down again and paid for it separately, with his own coins, so that it technically existed outside the budget. He felt this was clever. Later he would not feel that way.

Friday was the batch cooking. Seth browned the chicken in a pan that was too small, so the pieces steamed instead of seared, sweating palely in their own crowded steam like commuters on a hot bus. He portioned everything into five containers and slid four of them into the freezer chest at the back of the room, one marked for each day. Mr. Francis circled the room with his clipboard. He paused at Seth's station and said only, "Remember what we read about thawing," and moved on, because he was the kind of teacher who believed a person should arrive at his own disasters unassisted.

The trouble, as Seth reconstructed it, was that his freezer was extremely well organized, and the Monday container was at the back. On Sunday evening he meant to move it to the refrigerator. He thought about it at nine while brushing his teeth, at ten while pretending to read, and at some point after midnight, at which point he was asleep and thinking about nothing. He woke Monday to a container still in the freezer, frozen through, and a school departure time forty minutes away.

He set the container on the counter while he showered, which was, he told himself, a staging decision, a matter of workflow. Twenty minutes later the chicken was still hard as a paving stone and the surface had gone damp and faintly warm where the sun from the window touched it. Seth stared at it. Somewhere in the back of his mind, in Mr. Francis's dry voice, was the sentence from the handout, the one Seth had skimmed and assumed he'd remember by instinct: frozen food thaws safely in the refrigerator, in cold water, or in the microwave, but never by sitting out on the counter. Never by sitting out. He looked at the counter. He looked at the chicken sitting on it.

He was not, he conceded privately, going to beseech the chicken to thaw faster, though he considered it. The refrigerator would take all day and the meal was due at fourth period. That left two options, and he had time for one. He filled the sink with cold water, sealed the container inside a zip bag Edward had pressed on him Friday with the words "you'll need this, trust me," and submerged it, weighing the whole thing down with a pot so it wouldn't bob. Then he stood there in his towel, watching a bag of future lunch float in a sink, feeling less like a planner by nature and more like a person whose plan had been carried, mostly intact, by other people's foresight.

At school, Mr. Francis asked each of them to say one thing the week had taught them. Yann said something about unit prices. Edward said something about mise en place, which Seth suspected Edward had rehearsed. Seth stood up, opened his mouth to describe his "comprehensive food safety protocol," and then closed it again. He sat down without saying anything, and under the table, in the cooler he'd carried the thawed chicken in, the ice packs shifted against the container with a small, settling clink.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Blocking is the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage, set by the director during rehearsals.
story:
The debate tournament had spread itself across the whole of Marchmont High, and by noon Jack had already dropped his second round, on a resolution he secretly thought was unwinnable anyway. Between rounds he wandered the auxiliary corridor, the one normally used for storage, and heard voices through a propped door. Inside, three students stood on a taped-out rectangle of floor meant to be a stage, arguing about who was supposed to be where. One of them was Carmen, whom he knew from English, and she had her script rolled in her fist like a weapon.

"You crossed in front of me," the boy playing the father said. "The audience couldn't see my face for half the scene."

"I was reacting," the girl said. "That's my line to react on."

Jack lingered in the doorway, and Carmen noticed him. "It's a one-act," she said, half apology, half dare. "We perform it in three weeks at the community theatre. Don't you have a round?"

"Not till one." He watched the two actors walk the scene again, and again they collided near the imaginary kitchen table, the girl apologizing mid-sentence, the boy throwing up his hands. "You're moving them line by line," Jack said, before he quite decided to speak.

Carmen looked at him for a long moment. "They're actors. They move themselves."

"Ms. Levy says otherwise," said the boy. "She's the one who gave us the space. She said a director sets the movement."

"Sets it how?" Carmen asked, and Jack admitted he didn't know, only that he'd seen it in a rehearsal once, a director with a pencil, marking little arrows in the margins while actors stood still and waited. He had thought it looked tyrannical at the time, a pedagate's dream of control. Now, watching the two actors bump shoulders for the fourth time, he wondered if it was the opposite: if the arrows were a way of caring for them, of making sure no one's moment got hidden.

"Okay," Carmen said. "Direct us. You have forty minutes."

He laughed. She didn't. She handed him her copy of the script, and Jack stood where an audience would be, and for a while he simply watched, because he didn't yet trust himself to decide anything. Then he asked the girl to cross downstage on her line instead of upstage, and asked the father to stay planted by the table, and something happened that startled him: the scene made sense. The movement carried the argument. The girl's crossing toward the door meant she was leaving him; it had meant nothing when she'd drifted there at random.

From the back of the room, Carmen watched Jack work and felt something loosening and tightening in her chest at once. She had written the one-act herself, had fought the drama teacher to stage it, had cast these two friends because she trusted them, and had discovered in rehearsal that trust was not the same as a plan. Her deepest want, though she had told no one, was to hear an audience laugh at the joke on page six, the one about her grandmother's couch, because then she would know that the things she noticed about people were worth noticing. Every collision in scene two had felt like a small demolition of that hope, an audience being eviscerated out of the room one bump at a time. Now, under Jack's halting instructions, her actors moved like people who knew what they wanted, and she caught herself standing very still so as not to disturb it.

"Scene two, from the top," Jack said. "Sam, when she says the line about the hospital, don't move. Let her come to you." He had begun to see that stillness was a choice too, that deciding someone should not move was as strong a statement as any cross.

They ran it. The girl entered, the father stayed, the table sat invisible and solid between them, and when the girl said the line about the hospital, the whole taped rectangle seemed to hold its breath. Carmen, in the back, pressed her script against her ribs.

"Was that good or was that just us thinking it was good?" the girl asked.

"That's what the audience is for," Jack said. "Finding out."

When the forty minutes were up, Jack had to run for his third round, and he debated a girl from Westfield on economic sanctions, and lost again, and found he minded much less than he had expected to. On the bus home he kept seeing the taped floor in his mind, the arrows he would have drawn if he'd had a pencil, and he understood that the round he'd lost and the scene he'd watched were both arguments about where people stand, and who gets to decide. In debate he'd been taught to make the choice for the judge. In the black box theatre, Jack had spent forty minutes making choices for people he could not control, and the choices only worked because they walked toward them and made the choices their own. He could not yet say how those two things fit together, whether a director was closer to a debater or to something else, and he was honest enough with himself to leave the question open.

On Monday Carmen found him at lunch and slid a page across the table: the script, its margins now crowded with her own arrows, in pencil, small and deliberate. "Tuesday, four o'clock," she said. "Sam wants to try a different entrance. Come tell us if it's wrong."

Jack turned the page, reading the little diagrams of bodies and doors. "And if it's right?"

"Then tell us that too." She gathered her fries and stood, already halfway back toward the table where her actors waited, and he watched her go with the script still warm in his hand.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under the legal rule called contra proferentem, used in many jurisdictions, an ambiguous term in a contract is usually read against the party that wrote it.
story:
The charge appeared on a Thursday, seventeen dollars and forty cents under the heading "Activation Services," though Mya had activated nothing. She sat at the desk in her room with the laptop open to the phone company's customer portal, her contract email pinned in another tab, and a mug of tea going cold beside the mouse. At the bottom of the contract, in a font two sizes smaller than the rest, ran a line she must have scrolled past in June when she signed: "Activation and related services may be billed at the company's discretion." She read it three times, and it told her nothing about which services, or when, or how much.

She had until the first of the month, nine days, before the charge would pass into her payment history and, according to a forum she'd found, become much harder to dispute. Her mother had said, over dinner, that it was seventeen dollars, that the time she'd spend on it would cost more than that, and Mya had nodded and kept eating.
