But the seventeen dollars was not really the thing. The thing was that a company with a logo like a sunrise had written a sentence so vague it could mean anything, and she had signed under it, and she wanted to know whether signing meant agreeing to whatever they later decided the sentence meant.

She called Naomi, who was already at college two states away and answered on speaker while unpacking boxes. "Read me the line," Naomi said, and Mya read it. "That's not a term, that's a mood," Naomi said. "Ask them what 'related services' covers. Make them define it in writing." Mya opened the chat window on the portal and typed the question. The agent who answered, after eleven minutes, pasted back the same sentence, verbatim, as though it were its own explanation.

That evening Mr. Dlamini from next door was out watering his tomatoes, and Mya stopped at the fence on her way back from the mailbox. He had spent thirty years drafting agreements for a water utility, and he had a saturnine way of speaking about contracts, as if each one were a small grief. She told him about the line. He asked one question: "Who wrote it?" She said the company had. He looked at her over the fence for a moment, watering can tilted, and said only, "Then it's their sentence. Look up what courts do with a sentence like that." He went back to his tomatoes, and she understood that this was the whole of the help he intended to give.

Upstairs, she searched. It took her a while to find the phrase, buried in a plain-language guide to contract law, and when she found it she read it aloud to herself in the quiet room. "Contra proferentem," she said slowly, testing it. Under that rule, an ambiguous term in a contract is usually read against the party that wrote it. She sat with that for a moment. The company had drafted the sentence; the vagueness was theirs, and a court would not let them stretch it over whatever they wanted to aggrandize their revenue. The ambiguity landed on their side of the fence, not hers.

Still, she was honest enough with herself to hold two ideas at once. The rule was about courts, and she was not in a court; she was one eighteen-year-old with a chat window and a deadline. Maybe the company would ignore her. Maybe "usually" was doing a lot of work in that sentence. She drafted the message anyway, twice, the first version too sharp, the second one calm: she cited the exact wording, stated that the term was ambiguous as applied to her account, that she had not requested any activation or related service, and that she expected the charge reversed before the first. At the end she added, plainly, without lecture, "Under contra proferentem, an ambiguous term is read against the party that wrote it."

She sent it at 10:42 that night and slept badly, checking the portal at 6 a.m., then again after breakfast. At noon on Saturday the reply came, not from the chat agent but from a department called Billing Resolution. The charge had been reviewed and would be reversed within two billing cycles. Below that, a single human sentence: "We appreciate you citing the applicable principle." Mya read it twice, aware that she could not tell whether she had been heard or merely processed, whether the rule had moved them or the paperwork had simply found its level, the way water does, seeking the lowest place, patient as an aquifer under dry ground.

When Naomi called that evening, Mya told her the whole sequence, including the part she still couldn't explain. "Seventeen dollars," Naomi said, laughing a little. "You fought a phone company over seventeen dollars." Mya looked at the reversal notice still open on the screen, at the small green check beside it, and said, "It was their sentence."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: In 2023, the US unemployment rate was 3.9 percent for workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma and 5.6 percent for those without one.
story:
William found Jude sitting on the hood of a rusted Civic at the far edge of the parking lot, still in his gown but with the cap folded in his lap like something he was deciding whether to keep. The ceremony had let out twenty minutes ago, and families were clustered near the entrance taking photographs, their laughter carrying across the asphalt in bright, scattered bursts. Jude had no family there. He had dropped out in November of junior year and come anyway, because Mr. Chukwu had mailed him an invitation with a note that said the school considered him one of theirs, whatever the registrar's file said.

"You look like a judge," Jude said, nodding at the gown. "Like you're about to sentence somebody."

"I feel like a costume that hasn't decided what it is." William sat down beside him, the metal warm through the fabric. He had known Jude since seventh grade, when they'd been the two boys who took the bus transfer at the same stop, and he still didn't know how to begin, so he began with the small thing. "I got the scholarship. The partial one."

"I heard. Murray told me." Jude turned the cap over in his hands. "That's good, Will. That's actually good." Then, quieter, in the voice he used when he was about to admit something: "I've put in forty-one applications since January. I counted. Forty-one. Grocery stores, the distribution center out past the highway, two restaurants, the car wash. I got three interviews and one shift at the car wash before they cut hours."

William had his phone out before he thought about whether it was rude. He typed slowly, wanting to get the search right, and the numbers came up faster than he expected. He read them twice, then a third time, because they seemed to say something he hadn't known how to hold before. "Jude. Listen to this. Last year, 2023. For workers twenty-five and older with a high school diploma, unemployment was 3.9 percent. For people without one, 5.6."

Jude looked at the screen, then at him. "So it's not just me."

"It's not just you. It's the paper, too. It's both." William lowered the phone. He had spent two years believing, in the vague way he believed things he'd never had to test, that the diploma was mostly a ritual, that what mattered was working hard, and Jude had worked hard, harder than William some semesters. But the numbers sat there and refused to dissolve into that comfortable idea. At the same time, 3.9 wasn't zero. A diploma wasn't a door, only a slightly better set of odds, and he understood suddenly that he had been treating it as more than that because it was the thing he happened to have.

From where Jude sat, the graduation crowd looked almost cosmopolitan, the way it did in the school's brochure photographs: families in bright formal clothes, an uncle in a suit from Lagos beside a grandmother in a church hat, someone's cousin videoing everything in Portuguese. He had wanted to be in those pictures. That was the honest version, the one he could say now to this particular person, because William had never once made him feel like a cautionary tale. "I keep thinking about my dad," Jude said. "He didn't finish school either, back home. He calls the shop his patrimony, like it's land he's passing down. Four hundred square feet of tires and a hydraulic lift. And I can't even get the car wash to keep me."

"You could do the GED," William said, and then heard how it sounded, like something a guidance counselor would enunciate slowly at a kid who'd made a mistake. He tried again, plainer. "Or Murray's uncle at the distribution center. Murray said they train people. Either way it's not the whole answer, I know that. The numbers aren't the whole answer either. I don't actually know how much of anything I know right now."

Jude laughed, a real one, short and surprised. "That's the most anyone's said to me all year. Everyone else has a plan for me." He slid off the hood and stood, brushing off his jeans, and for a moment he held the folded cap out at arm's length, considering it. Then he set it gently on the hood, squared it up like something returned rather than abandoned.

Mr. Chukwu came across the lot with his clipboard still under his arm, tie loosened, and stopped a few feet away, catching his breath. "Jude. I hoped you'd stayed." He looked at the cap on the hood and didn't reach for it, didn't comment, just stood with them while a family nearby erupted in cheering for a boy who had tripped on his gown and gotten up laughing. "The bus doesn't run this route after six," he said finally. "Either of you need a ride?"

"We're good," Jude said. "We're walking to Murray's. He's got a thing going with the grill." He picked the cap back up, unfolded it, and put it on, tugging the brim low. "Okay if I wear it one more block?"

"Keep it," Mr. Chukwu said. "It's yours. It was always going to be yours."

They crossed the lot together, William still in his gown and Jude in the cap, their shadows stretching long and doubled on the asphalt, and Jude said, "So tell me about this partial scholarship, but this time tell me the parts you left out."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge.
story:
Brody got to the park twenty minutes early, which he decided was seventeen minutes too early, so he walked a slow loop past the duck pond and tried to look like a person who happened to be there. He had texted Gaelle the night before, saying the old suspension footbridge over the ravine, the one with the ice cream cart near it, six o'clock, and she had replied with a single thumbs up that he had then read eleven times. In his back pocket he carried two tickets to the nine o'clock horror screening at the rep cinema, which his friend Guillaume had insisted was a genius plan.

"Scary movie on a first date," Guillaume had said, clapping him on the shoulder in the locker room. "Her heart's pounding, she's grabbing your arm, she thinks it's you. Chemistry does the work. You just stand there."

Brody had doubted it in a vague way, the way he doubted most of Guillaume's certainties, but he took the tickets anyway, because Guillaume had bought them as a favor and wanted badly to be the kind of friend who arranged things, who could say later that he had made it happen. That want was louder than Brody's doubt, so the doubt lost, as it usually did.

Gaelle arrived at two minutes past six, sandals slapping the path, carrying a paper cup of lemonade she'd bought from the cart. She was in his chem class and had corrected his enthalpy calculations twice in one lab, both times without making him feel stupid, which was more than he could say for the textbook. They stood a moment in the sun and she said, "So you picked a bridge."

"It's the best thing in this park. Objectively." He said it in a facetious tone, chin up, and she laughed, so he counted that as a point.

They walked out onto the span together. It was old, the kind that swayed when a jogger passed and hummed under wind, cables strung loose as guitar strings gone dull. Halfway across, Gaelle stopped and put a hand on the rail. "I hate this part," she said. "Not the height. The way it moves after you've stopped."

"Like it's deciding without you."

"Don't make it poetic or I'll push you off." But she was smiling, and her free hand had found his sleeve.

A jogger thundered past and the deck rolled under them, a long slow sway that made both of them grab the rail, and when it settled they were laughing, breathless, and Brody could feel his own heart going hard against his ribs. Here was the thing he wanted to say, and he turned it over once before saying it, because there were two ways to hold it. One was Guillaume's way: use it, stack the deck, let the swaying bridge do the work of making her feel something and take the credit. The other felt more honest but smaller.

"There's this study," he said. "From 1974, these psychologists, Dutton and Aron. Guys who had just crossed a scary suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than guys who crossed a sturdy bridge."

"Call her?"

"Afterward. She'd given them her number for, like, follow-up questions. The scared guys called."

Gaelle looked at him, then out at the ravine. "And you're telling me this on a bridge."

"I'm telling you this on a bridge because I want you to know my heart's hammering and I don't fully know why. Could be you. Could be the swaying. The study says the wires get crossed." He let go of the rail, and his hand was shaking slightly, which undercut the whole speech. "Guillaume said to take you to a horror movie and let the movie do it. I bought the tickets before I decided I hated that plan."

"Because it's sneaky?"

"Because it's sneaky and because if it worked I'd never know if it was real. I'd just be aggrandizing a chemical mix-up into a whole thing." The word came out bigger than he intended, but she didn't flinch.

She took a slow sip of her lemonade. There was a long quiet in which the bridge kept up its low hum, and somewhere below them a kid threw stones into the creek. Brody watched her not look at him and thought, with real cold clarity, that there was no clean answer even now. Even telling her the study was a move. Even honesty could be a strategy if you used it at the right moment, and he had used it at this one.

"Okay," Gaelle said finally. "Two things. One, I'm scared of this bridge too, genuinely, since I was like eight, so we're in it together and neither of us gets to know. Two." She held out the lemonade. "Hold this."

He took the cup. She walked three planks ahead, to where the deck was widest, and stood there with her arms out, waiting for the next jogger.

When the bridge bucked under the footsteps, she grabbed the rail and whooped, and the sound went up the ravine and came back off the far wall. Then she looked over her shoulder at him, hair across her face, cup of lemonade still in his hand, and said, "Still scared?"

"Terrified," Brody called back, and started toward her.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way for a person to know whether they have one.
story:
Joshua had agreed to co-lead Friday's health workshop before he understood what he had agreed to. Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya had pitched it gently, the way he pitched everything, as though handing over a delicate parcel: senior students explaining consent, contraception and clinic testing to the Year Tens, because, he said, "they listen to you in a way they will never listen to me." Which was flattering for exactly one afternoon, until Joshua sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with a stack of pamphlets and realised he could not say any of it out loud without his voice doing something strange.

The grandparents' house was the only quiet place available. His own house held a younger brother who repeated everything he heard at volume, and the library smelled like the radiator was dying. Here there was the long table, the ticking clock, and his grandfather in the armchair with the newspaper, phlegmatic as a stone in a stream, letting the fuss of the household pass over him. Joshua spread out the pamphlets: one about consent, one about condoms and the pill and other methods, one from the downtown clinic about testing.

He began reading aloud, quietly, just to get his mouth around the words. Consent was first, and it was easier than he'd feared: clear, freely given, something you could withdraw, something silence did not supply. He practised phrasing it three ways. His grandfather rustled the paper and said, without looking up, "Slower on the second bit. You swallowed it." Joshua said it again, slower, feeling absurd and also, somehow, steadier.

Then he texted Yuna, who was supposed to be helping, and got back: I'm in. But Mariam says she doesn't need the testing part because she feels completely fine, so we can cut it?? Joshua stared at that. He picked up the clinic pamphlet and read it properly for the first time, and there it was, plain as anything: chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way for a person to know whether they have one. He read the sentence twice. Feeling fine, it turned out, proved nothing at all. He typed back, Testing stays in. Feeling fine isn't proof. It's in the clinic's own pamphlet. Yuna replied with three exclamation marks and a photo of Mariam looking sheepish, which did not augur well for Friday but at least meant the argument was happening now instead of in front of thirty fifteen-year-olds.

"So what does this word do," his grandfather said, tapping a finger on the contraception pamphlet. Joshua explained condoms, the pill, the implant, the injection, how each worked in the most basic terms, how no method was perfect, how two methods beat one. His grandfather nodded along, asked whether the implant hurt, and then, as Joshua reached for the testing pamphlet, said, "You'll want the phone number facing out. People take the number and pretend they're reading the rest."

Joshua looked up. "How do you know that?"

His grandfather folded the newspaper with great ceremony. "I drove the clinic van for six years after I retired. Every Thursday. You think I didn't learn anything from the seat of a van." He had never once mentioned this. Joshua's grandmother, appearing with tea, added that she had done the intake forms for three of those years, which was the twist of the day: the two people he'd been treating as scenery had run a mobile sexual health service out of a van with a squeaky fan belt. "Your granddad was famous for it," she said. "The boys from the college would come specifically when he was driving. Said he never made a face at anyone."

"The skill," his grandfather said, "is you hand them the form and you look at the door. Not at them. The door."

They drilled him until the light went amber in the window. His grandmother played a doubtful Year Ten, folding her arms and saying she felt fine, and Joshua said the line, "Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so a test is the only reliable way to know," and she said, "Good, now say it like you're not reciting a spell." He said it plainer the second time, and she nodded once, which in her currency was a standing ovation. His grandfather invented a nemesis for him, a heckler named Kevin who insisted the clinic reported everything to parents, and made Joshua answer him twice with the confidentiality rules until the answers came out steady.

On Thursday night Yuna called, panicked: Mariam had booked an appointment. Not because of anything dramatic; she'd read the pamphlet photo Yuna sent, thought about the word reliable, and decided that knowing was better than feeling fine. "She's taking me with her," Yuna said. "For the bus part. Hold on, she wants to tell you something."

Mariam's voice came on, small and dry. "Tell your granddad his van stories better be true, because I'm going to ask at reception."

His grandfather, listening from the armchair with hearing aids that missed nothing, said, "Tell her the fan belt squeaked and I never once made a face."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025 recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, a record for a single month.
story:
Maelle ironed the volunteer shirt twice before she realized it didn't need ironing, then folded it into her backpack anyway, because a folded shirt implied a plan and she wanted to have one. Her mother called from the kitchen that the bus came at 8:40, not 8:45, and Maelle said she knew, and then checked the schedule to confirm that she did not. The food bank ran out of a church basement ten minutes from their street, and she had walked past it her whole life without once looking at the door.

Rowan was already there, stacking cans with the insouciant efficiency of someone who had done it a hundred times and found it boring in a way he clearly enjoyed performing. "You came," he said. "I told Alice you'd bail."

"I didn't bail."

"You bailed on the hike."

"The hike was rained out."

"See, that's bailing with an alibi." He handed her a crate of pasta. "Pasta goes on the left wall. It's a whole system. The coordinator will explain it in a voice like she's teaching kindergarten."

The coordinator did not sound like kindergarten. She sounded tired in a way that had stopped being temporary, and she explained the line, the intake table, the list of what each household could take, and then said, "Saturday's our big day, but don't underestimate a Tuesday." Rowan laughed, a short sound with no humor in it. "My mom showed me the HungerCount numbers," he said while they rolled a cart toward the door. "Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025. Nearly 2.2 million visits in one month, March 2025. A record for a single month, in the whole country." Maelle said that couldn't be right, that many people, and Rowan said, "Look it up when your phone dies of boredom," and rolled the cart through the swinging door.

The line went past the coat rack and out into the stairwell. She had imagined the food bank as something quiet and manageable, a few elderly people, a young mother maybe, the scene she had assembled from donation bins at school. What she got instead was a Tuesday morning line that did not move for the first ten minutes, and her job was to stand at the intake table and say hello and ask how many people were in the household, and to mark it down, and to not look at anyone longer than the form required. She was bad at the not-looking. A man around her father's age held his list with both hands like a test he hadn't studied for, and she wanted to say something that would fix it, and there was nothing on the table that was that.

At eleven the line thinned and the third man in the last small group set his basket down, and she saw it was Mr. Demir, who had lived four doors down until she was twelve, who had taught her to parallel park between his car and the hydrant using traffic cones and an alarming amount of shouting. He recognized her at the same moment. "Maelle," he said. "You've grown sideways into a clipboard."

"Mr. Demir."

"Two in the household," he said, "if you need it for the form," and he said it evenly, without apology, which somehow made her throat tighten more than an apology would have. She marked the two. He took his rice and his cans and said, "The cones are still in my garage, if you ever want practice," and then he was past the table and gone, and she stood there holding the pen.

She thought about it all through the lunch break, which the volunteers took on folding chairs behind the freezer. In her head there were two versions of the morning and neither would sit still. One said the line was a system failure, a number, something to be argued about with other numbers; Rowan's 2.2 million belonged to that version, and she understood why he'd memorized it, the way you memorize a statistic to make a feeling portable. The other version was Mr. Demir saying "two in the household" while she wrote it down, and that was not a number at all, it was a phenomenology of shame and pride folded together, the specific weight of being known by a neighbor at the worst possible table. She had always assumed those two ways of seeing were rivals, that you had to pick the spreadsheet or the face, and it was occurring to her now, uncomfortably, that they might be the same obligation wearing different clothes. What stayed uncertain was whether she was doing anything at all, whether handing a man rice and pretending not to know him helped or just catalyzed her own sense of being a decent person, a small chemical reaction in which he was the reagent and she got to feel the warmth.

Rowan sat down beside her with a sandwich. "Your old teacher?"

"Neighbor. He taught me to park."

"That's a twist." He ate for a while. "You'll come back, right? Alice bet you wouldn't, but I told her the clipboard would get you. It gets everyone."

"It hasn't gotten you. You're bored."

"I'm not bored, I'm efficient," he said, and stole her apple, and the afternoon line began to form at the door.

She walked home past the church and past Mr. Demir's old house, now someone else's, with a different car in the driveway. Her mother asked how it went, and Maelle said, "I'm going back Tuesday," and went to fold the shirt for next week.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Under the two-second rule, a driver watches the car ahead pass a fixed point, such as a sign, and checks that at least two seconds pass before reaching that same point.
story:
Violet's father had surrendered the driver's seat with the solemnity of a man handing over the keys to a bank vault, and now he sat in the back between Louis-Philippe and Pierre, arms crossed, pretending to read a gum wrapper. Ms. Lawson settled into the passenger seat, adjusted the mirror with two fingers, and said, "Whenever you're ready, dear. It's a quiet street. The worst that can happen is mild humiliation."

"Comforting," said Violet. Her hands found ten and two, the way the booklet had insisted, and the car lurched forward, hesitated, lurched again, like a horse deciding whether it liked her. Pierre made a sound like a dial-up modem. Louis-Philippe applauded softly, three slow claps, which felt worse than booing.

"Smooth," her father offered from the back, in the tone of a man who had reified the phrase backseat driver into an entire personality. "Very smooth. Like a milkshake."

They crawled toward the ring road, and the problem announced itself gradually, the way problems do. Violet kept drifting toward the car ahead, a green hatchback with a stick-figure family on the rear window, two adults, four children, one dog. Each time she noticed, she braked too hard, and everyone tipped forward in a gentle wave, and then she crept up again. Her father leaned between the seats. "You're tailgating a station wagon full of fictional children, Violet."

"I know. I'm fixing it."

"You're fixing it the way a cat fixes a vase."

Ms. Lawson raised one hand, and the car went respectfully quiet. "You're not doing anything wrong that a million learners haven't done. You want to be close because close feels like control." She pointed through the windshield at an approaching lamppost. "Ask your friend there. The one who failed his test twice."

"Once," said Pierre. "The first one was a clerical error. Chicanery at the test centre." But he leaned forward, hooked his chin over the seat, and said, "Two-second rule. Watch the car ahead. When it passes something fixed, a sign, a lamppost, whatever, you count the seconds until you reach that same point. You want at least two."

"So I count from the lamppost," Violet said slowly, "and I should get to two before I get to the lamppost."

"Give or take."

The green hatchback rolled past the next lamppost. "One Mississippi, two Mississippi," Violet said, and then the lamppost slid by her window, arriving far too early, almost on the second word. "That's bad, right?"

"That's you eating its bumper," said Louis-Philippe.

She eased off the accelerator, experimentally, the way you test a loose tooth. At the following sign she counted again. One Mississippi. Two Mississippi. She crossed the sign's shadow a heartbeat after two, and something in her chest unclenched, a knot she hadn't known she was tying. The road ahead opened up into a corridor of lampposts, and she found she could hold her distance by counting against them, a rhythm underneath the driving, steadier than her nerves.

"It's weird," she said. "It's like the gap became a thing. Before, it was just air and panic, and now it's two seconds. I can count it." She was aware, even as she said it, that this was the kind of thinking she'd been warned about in English class, turning a feeling into an object so you could hold it, and she was also aware that it was working, so philosophy could wait.

"Mind the cyclist," said her father, and everyone's head swivelled at once, a family of meerkats, and Violet slowed, signalled wide, and counted her way past him too.

At the roundabout she stalled the engine. The car behind honked, Louis-Philippe honked back using only his mouth, and Ms. Lawson laughed until she had to wipe her eye. Violet restarted, checked the mirror, and pulled out into traffic, leaving what she judged, counting, to be rather more than two seconds of space, possibly three, possibly, at one gliding moment, four.

"Better too many seconds than too few," she said.

"Listen to her," said her father. "Six hours behind the wheel and she's already quoting herself."

They turned for home as the streetlights came on, one after another down the avenue, and Violet counted past each of them without needing to, out of habit, out of delight, a small pulse of numbers keeping the whole lit world at a tenable distance.

"Same time Thursday?" said Ms. Lawson.

"Book it," said Violet, and took the last corner wide and slow, the indicator ticking like a calm little clock.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing.
story:
The field behind the middle school had been reconditioned that spring, and by July the outfield grass was still patchy in the corners, so Maika played left with one eye on the ball and one on the brown spots that could turn a routine single into a triple. She had joined the summer league in May because her mother said she needed something that wasn't the library, and she had stayed because, against all expectation, she could hit. The team was a mixed squad, girls from three different schools, and for the first weeks they had all been careful with one another, passing the sunflower seeds around, learning names, laughing politely at jokes that weren't funny yet.

Then, in the last week of June, the carefulness wore through. Katerina, who pitched, lambasted the shortstop after a dropped pop fly in a game they lost by two, and the shortstop, whose name was Brennen, said something back that Maika didn't catch but that made Katerina's face go stiff. The next practice, nobody passed the seeds. Maika found herself standing in the same six feet of outfield she always stood in, listening to the infield argue about whether the cutoff should be the second baseman or the shortstop, and thinking that the argument wasn't really about cutoffs at all.

"We were nicer when we were worse," she said to Katerina on the walk to the bus stop, the equipment bag dragging between them.

"That's not a real observation," Katerina said, but she said it tiredly, without heat, which meant she'd been thinking something similar.

The breaking point came at Tuesday practice. Brennen showed up fifteen minutes late, and the third baseman told her where she could put her glove, and it would have become a real fight if Ms. Njoroge hadn't called everyone in to the mound. Maika expected a lecture, the kind adults gave about attitude and commitment, and she braced for it. Instead Ms. Njoroge stood there with her hands in the pockets of her windbreaker and said, "Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing. First you're polite, then you fight. We're storming." She said it flatly, like a score, and then pointed at the bucket of balls and told Katerina to pitch.

Maika thought about it all the way home and again in the shower and again in bed, where she looked it up on her laptop to see if Ms. Njoroge had made it up. She hadn't. Four stages, an actual taxonomy, decades old. She read the words forming and storming and felt the small satisfaction of having a name for a thing, and then the unsatisfying part: the name didn't tell you what to do. The stages told you the team was somewhere along a road, but not how far, and not whether knowing about the road made it any shorter. She had assumed, before, that a team either worked or didn't, that chemistry was a kind of luck. This was a different way of thinking, and she couldn't decide yet whether it was more tenable than luck or just more comforting.

She was still deciding three days later, in the dugout before a doubleheader, when the storming arrived on schedule. Brennen and the catcher got into it over signs, quietly at first, then not quietly, and Maika watched the rest of the team split into glances, everyone deciding whose side to be on without moving from the bench. Katerina was at the far end, chalking her cleats, pretending not to listen.

Katerina had her own version of the last month, which she was not in the habit of saying out loud. From where she sat, the whole mess had started the day she'd yelled at Brennen, which meant it was hers to close. She had heard Ms. Njoroge's line about 1965 and found it a little too tidy, teams weren't caterpillars, but she'd also noticed that nobody had spoken to Brennen directly since the dropped ball, that the whole team had been conducting an argument through positioning drills and silence. She got up, walked the length of the dugout, and sat down next to Brennen with the chalk still on her hands. "The signs thing," she said. "You're right about the one finger. I've been shaking off half your calls."

Brennen looked at her for a second, then at the chalk dust Katerina had left on the bench between them. "Two fingers is the changeup," she said. "If I call two, throw whatever you want."

From third base coaching box, Ms. Njoroge watched the two of them laughing at something and made a small note on her lineup card, which was not about the lineup. Maika, watching from the on-deck circle, felt the two ways of thinking settle against each other: the neat four-stage ladder, and the messier truth that the ladder didn't climb itself, that someone still had to stand up and cross a dugout. Maybe the stages were real and so was the choice. She held both ideas the way she held the bat, loosely, ready.

In the second game they turned two double plays and Katerina threw a changeup on a two-finger call that froze the cleanup hitter so completely the umpire's strike call seemed almost cruel. Afterward, unlacing her cleats by the fence, Maika heard Brennen telling the catcher, "See, that's the norming," and the catcher saying, "That's not a word," and Brennen saying it absolutely was, and Maika looked out at the patchy outfield and decided she'd take first base coaching next season if it was offered.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 1990 follow-up of Mischel's preschoolers found that those who had waited longer for the second treat tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers.
story:
The packet in Nevaeh's tote bag was already heavy with pamphlets, and she had circled nothing. Her mother had circled everything. "You said you'd decide by four," her mother said, checking her phone in the lobby of the science building, where a banner read EXPLORE YOUR FUTURE in letters that struck Nevaeh as evanescent, the way futures tended to be when you got close to them.

Jalen had come on the same bus from their high school, and he wanted the neuroscience tables while Nevaeh had been steered, for two years now, toward the guaranteed-admission medical program. The application was due Monday. If she filed it, her next eight years were mapped: the same university, the same city, a seat held open for her in a lecture hall she was standing in right now.

At the psychology department's table, a man in a faculty polo was handing out marshmallows from a bag, a joke Nevaeh didn't get until he said, "The marshmallow test, of course." A parent beside him, a father with a lanyard and a tired blazer, laughed and turned to his daughter. "You know this one. Mischel's study. The preschoolers who could wait for the second marshmallow instead of eating the first one." His daughter rolled her eyes with a fluency that suggested years of practice. "And in 1990," the father went on, "they did a follow-up. The kids who'd waited longer as preschoolers tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers."

"Which means I'm doomed," the daughter said, "because I ate the marshmallow." She said it lightly, but Nevaeh noticed she didn't laugh, and neither did her father, who offered the consolation that it was only a tendency, only tended, and then got distracted by a flyer about housing.

Nevaeh drifted toward Jalen, who was spinning a brain-shaped stress ball on his finger. She told him what she'd overheard. "So one afternoon when you're four predicts your SATs," she said. "One afternoon predicts fourteen years." Jalen shrugged. "Or it doesn't. Tended. That's a weasel word if I've ever heard one." "It's a statistics word," Nevaeh said. "It's not the same thing as a promise."

They walked into the next session, a panel in a room where the air conditioning labored audibly. Ms. Rao, their AP Chemistry teacher, had driven up for the day and was sitting three rows ahead; she caught Nevaeh's eye and pointed at a seat beside her, and Nevaeh sat, because sitting beside Ms. Rao was easier than explaining why she had come to a panel called Interdisciplinary Pathways in the Arts and Sciences when her mother believed she was at the medical school tour.

During the question period a student asked whether switching directions after committing to a program stigmatized you in front of admissions committees. The moderator said something diplomatic about growth. Nevaeh wrote nothing down. She kept thinking about the preschoolers, the two treats, the long gap between the waiting and the follow-up, and about how the father had said only a tendency, and how a tendency was not a sentence but it was also not nothing.

Afterward, in the corridor, her mother texted: Filled out the program card yet? The card was in Nevaeh's bag, half-printed with her name and an address she'd lived at for eighteen years. She found Ms. Rao by the water fountain and asked her, without preamble, whether she thought a person could tell at seventeen what she'd want at twenty-five. Ms. Rao filled her cup slowly. "I think you already know I won't answer that." "You're an iconoclast, you're supposed to overturn things." "I overturn bad data," Ms. Rao said. "Decisions aren't data. They're more like the marshmallows. You only find out later what they were."

Jalen found them at the edge of the quad, where the tour groups were thinning toward the parking lots. Nevaeh took the program card out of her bag and looked at it, the little boxes, the signature line. She thought of the four-year-olds waiting, and of the teenagers with their scores, the whole long thread pulled tight between one moment and another, and she thought: the thread is real, but nobody ever says which end you're standing on. She borrowed a pen from Ms. Rao. Then she turned the card over to its blank side and wrote, at the top, Questions to ask before Monday, and underlined it twice. Jalen leaned over her shoulder. "What's the first one?" Nevaeh wrote it out: What am I waiting for, and is it worth it? "That's two questions," Jalen said. She handed him the pen. "Add yours, then."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: The Surrealist André Breton described Kahlo's art as "a ribbon around a bomb," though Kahlo herself later rejected the Surrealist label.
story:
Ava had told her mother the camp was mostly swimming, which was true in the sense that the lake existed and she had put her feet in it once. The rest of the time she was in a converted boathouse with nine other rising college freshmen and a poster of a Frida Kahlo painting taped to the easel that leaned against the wall because the nail had fallen out in June and nobody had fixed it since.

Mr. Sultani handed out the assignment on Tuesday. Formal analysis, he said, meaning colour, composition, symbolism, in that order or any order you like, but all three, and two pages, no biography, no feelings about her unibrow, and no word "soulmate" or he would fail you on the spot, which nobody believed, but nobody tested it either.

The painting was the one with the deer, a woman's face on a wounded animal body pierced by arrows, standing in a dry forest under a sky that couldn't decide what season it was. Eden, who sat beside Ava and chewed her pen cap into modern sculpture, leaned over and said, "Easy, it's Surrealism, dream logic, done." Ava wrote that down because Eden had taken AP Art History and Ava had taken AP Chemistry, and in Ava's private accounting of the world, people who could name a movement were ahead of people who could not.

Leighton disagreed, though not at first. At first Leighton said nothing and read a library book with a broken spine while everyone else argued about whether the arrows were "phallic," a word the boy across the table used four times until even he seemed tired of it. Then, when Eden repeated that the painting was straightforward Surrealism, Leighton looked up and said, "She rejected that label. Kahlo did. She said she painted her own reality, not dreams."

Eden asked how Leighton knew, and Leighton held up the book, and the book was about the Surrealists, and there it was in the index. André Breton had described her work as "a ribbon around a bomb." Ava copied the phrase onto her hand because her notebook was in the boathouse and the argument had moved outside, onto the dock, where the whole thing continued with more mosquitoes.

That night Ava lay on the top bunk in Cabin 4 and thought about the ribbon and the bomb, which was difficult because her bunkmate snored in a way that could reasonably be called structural. The phrase was a good one, she admitted, and it flattered the paintings, and it flattered the viewer too, because it made you feel clever for noticing that something decorative contained something destructive. But if the painter herself had refused the label, whose description was it, really? Breton's, obviously. It was Breton's description. The question was whether that mattered.

She got up, took the flashlight, and went down to the boathouse, which was unlocked because the padlock had been lost to the lake in July and Mr. Sultani had decided, philosophically, that nobody would steal a laminated poster. She sat on the floor in front of the deer and worked through her two pages in the flashlight beam, badly at first. She wrote that the sky was divided between warmth and storm, that the deer stood on one leg of the composition's implied triangle while the arrows pulled the eye across it, that the leaves were rendered with botanical precision while the wounds were rendered flat, like stickers. Then she crossed out "like stickers." Then she wrote it again.

Here is what Ava worked out, or half worked out, in the cold, with the flashlight dimming because she had not brought spare batteries because she was, her mother maintained, an optimist about equipment. Breton's phrase was accurate as a description of effect: the paint was the ribbon, the wound was the bomb. But calling the work Surrealist put it inside a movement, a little European polity with membership cards and manifestos, and Kahlo had declined the membership while keeping the wound. The painting did something Surrealism claimed to do, but it did it by insisting on the literal. The deer was not a dream deer. The arrows were arrows. The blood was blood, painted carefully, in a red that did not extenuate anything, that did not soften or spread blame, that just said, here is the red.

The next morning Ava turned in her two pages, and there was a paragraph at the end that she was not sure about, and she said so, in a footnote, in pen, which Mr. Sultani later called either honest or peevish, she couldn't tell which and decided not to ask. The footnote said: the ribbon/bomb line is Breton's, not hers, and if I use his words to describe her painting I should say I'm doing it, because he was describing her from the outside and she spent a career objecting to exactly that. She did not resolve whether the phrase could still be used. She put a question mark and left it.

Eden got her paper back with an A minus and the comment "good instincts, check your labels," and took it well, by which Ava means Eden said nothing for an hour and then made a joke about manifestos that landed harder than she probably intended. Leighton got an A and gave the library book to Ava without being asked, and Ava read the Breton chapter twice, once by the lake with her feet in the water, once in the boathouse after hours, where she sat cross-legged in front of the deer with the flashlight propped between two paint tins. On the last day of camp the nail was still missing and the poster was still leaning, and Ava took a photograph of it at an angle so it would look straight, and then, after looking at the photograph, deleted it and took one that showed the lean.

Mr. Sultani caught her on her way to the bus and said the footnoted question mark was the best thing in the paper. "The bomb part or the ribbon part?" Ava asked. He shrugged and handed her the padlock someone had finally fished out of the lake, rusted shut, good for nothing now except evidence. She put it in her pocket and carried it home.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The Maillard reaction, between amino acids and sugars, browns food and creates much of its flavor; it proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius.
story:
Isla had promised her family one proper dinner before Saturday, and by proper she meant the kind her grandmother used to make, the kind that made people go quiet at the table and then loud again with compliments. The chicken sat in the pan looking like something that had given up. Pale, slick, sweating in its own steam, it resembled a swimmer who had never once been in the sun.

"You've debilitated that bird," said her grandmother from the doorway, arms crossed over her cardigan. "It's not injured. It's just sad."

"It's cooked," Isla said. "The thermometer said so. Seventy-four degrees all the way through. Food-safe. Technically delicious."

Her grandmother came to stand at the stove and peered into the pan the way one peers at a crime scene. "Technically," she repeated, as though the word itself were the problem.

The plan had come together that afternoon in the school corridor, where Kristian had leaned against the lockers and declared that a person who could not cook would be a reactionary by the time she was thirty, afraid of every new thing in the kitchen. Mark had defended her, sort of, by saying that his entire diet was microwave noodles and he was thriving, which nobody believed, least of all Mark. Somewhere between those two positions Isla had decided on chicken, because chicken was what her grandmother made, and because Ms. Traoré had once mentioned, in the middle of a chemistry lesson that had seemed at the time to have nothing to do with anything, that cooking was chemistry you could eat. Isla had written it in the margin of her notebook and then forgotten it until the pale bird stared up at her from the pan.

Now she turned the heat up and stood guard while her grandmother told a story about a saturnine butcher in her old neighbourhood who never smiled, not once, not even when he dropped a whole tray of sausages, which in Isla's opinion was the single most smile-worthy event imaginable. The pan began to hiss. The bottom of the chicken went from blancmange to gold at the edges, then deeper, then brown with darker streaks in it, and the kitchen filled with a smell that had not been there before, savoury and a little sweet, the smell of the dinners she remembered.

"There it is," her grandmother said, as if the smell were a guest arriving.

"What is it, though?" Isla asked. "The smell. Where does it come from? It wasn't there before."

Her grandmother tapped the pan's handle with one knuckle. "Maillard reaction," she said. "Amino acids and sugars browning the food, making most of the flavour. It wants it hot, 140 to 165 degrees, and it goes fast."

Isla stared at her. "You know the chemistry?"

"I know the pan," her grandmother said. "Your Ms. Whatever-her-name is can know the chemistry."

The sentence rearranged something in Isla's head. She had been carrying two separate ideas around like coins in different pockets: on one side, the science from class, precise and true, with its numbers and its certainty; on the other, her grandmother's hands, which had never measured anything and which were never wrong. She had assumed they were rivals, or at least strangers to each other. Apparently they had been collaborating for sixty years. The thermometer in her pocket said the pan surface was now well past 165, too hot, so she eased the dial back down a notch, and the browning slowed to something gentler, still moving but no longer rushing, and she thought, not for the first time, that the world was mostly like this, two true things leaning on each other.

Mark arrived at the back door without knocking, because Mark never knocked, carrying a bag of oranges "as payment in advance" for a dinner he had not been invited to. Kristian followed, having texted Isla six increasingly dramatic messages about whether the chicken had survived. When they saw the second batch, the one in the properly hot pan, lifted onto a board with skin like lacquered wood, Mark set the oranges down and said nothing at all, which for Mark was a eulogy.

They ate at the table crowded and loud, Mark narrating his own chewing, Kristian proposing a toast "to heat, the ingredient we forgot," the grandmother allowing herself the smallest smile when the father went back for seconds without being asked. Isla ate slowly. She kept thinking about the first bird, still sitting in its pan on the stove, pale and safe and dull, and about the thin line between doing a thing correctly and doing it well, which she could not have drawn on paper if anyone had asked her to. Maybe the line moved. Maybe it depended on who was eating.

Afterward, alone in the kitchen with the washing-up, she scraped the pan and found the browned bits stuck to the bottom, the ones her grandmother had said never to throw away. She set the pan back on the flame, poured in a splash of water, and watched the dark sediment lift and swirl into something that smelled like the whole evening.

"Kristian!" she called toward the living room. "Come taste this. And bring an orange."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Johann Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, drawing on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel.
story:
The metronome had been in the garage since before Zoey was born, a wooden pyramid with a brass weight and a winding key, sitting on the closed lid of her grandmother's upright piano. She had never wound it until the night she decided she had to be good at bass guitar by Friday, which gave her six days, and the garage was the only place her parents couldn't hear her mistakes.

She set the weight to ninety and put her fingers on the E string. Tick, tick, tick. Her plucking lagged behind, then surged ahead, then lagged again, like two people trying to walk together who kept stepping on each other's heels. She stopped and stared at the machine. Somebody had to have invented this thing, this patient little device that made her failure audible every single second.

"Wasn't it Beethoven?" said Celina, who came over the next afternoon with her backpack still on, having heard about the audition at lunch. "Or, like, some German genius."

"Beethoven didn't invent machines," Zoey said. "He wrote music." But she wasn't sure, and it bothered her more than it should have. She was the kind of person who read the whole encyclopedia entry, who couldn't leave a question half answered, and here she was trusting a guess.

Celina tilted her phone screen toward the garage's single dusty window for better light. "Johann Maelzel," she read. "Patented the mechanical metronome in 1815." She scrolled. "Huh. But look, it says drawing on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel."

"So Maelzel took the credit," Zoey said slowly. "Winkel did the real work and Maelzel got the patent." Something about that sat wrong in her chest, or maybe right, she couldn't tell. She wound the instrument again and let it tick. "He stole it, kind of. Or borrowed it. Depending on how you look."

"That's such a Maelzel thing to do," Celina said, dropping onto an old paint bucket. "Take someone's idea, put your name on it, everyone claps."

But Zoey was already thinking past that, the way she did when a question had two doors. Winkel had the idea and Maelzel had made it exist for the whole world, patented it, manufactured it, put it in every practice room for the next two centuries. Without Maelzel, was there even a metronome on this piano? And yet Winkel's name was the one people forgot, and forgetting him felt like a small theft repeated ten million times. She couldn't decide which mattered more, the making or the spreading, and she didn't like not being able to decide.

Their neighbor Mr. Tremblay appeared at the open garage door that evening, drawn by the sound of the same four bars played forty times. He stood listening with a jaundiced expression, as though he expected very little and had rarely been disappointed. "Your grandmother taught herself on that piano," he said. "No lessons. Completely self-taught, an autodidact of the old kind. She'd have liked that you're using her metronome."

"I found out who invented it," Zoey said, mostly to keep him there. "Maelzel. 1815. Except really it was Winkel, and Maelzel just took the patent."

"History's full of that," Mr. Tremblay said. "Play the four bars again."

She played them. He shook his head at the third beat, and she played them again, and again, until her fingertips burned and the metronome ticked like a small heart she had to match. Two hours later she hit the passage clean, all four bars, locked to the pulse, and Celina, who had come back with snacks, actually set the snacks down without eating any, which was the highest compliment she could pay.

The audition Friday was in the school gym, three minutes per person, and Zoey got called while her hands were still cold. The judge, a bored man with a clipboard, said, "Whenever you're ready." There was no metronome in the gym, but she could hear it anyway, ticking at ninety inside her, and she thought briefly of Winkel, unremembered, and of Maelzel, remembered perhaps too much, and decided the honest position was that she didn't know which of them deserved the applause and that she was going to play anyway. She set her fingers on the E string.

Afterward Celina was quiet on the walk out, which terrified Zoey more than any score could have. Then Celina said, "You dragged on the bridge section."

"I know," Zoey said. "My tempo slipped. I heard it."

"Want to go back to the garage and fix it?"

Zoey shifted the case strap on her shoulder. "Wound and waiting," she said.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but it acts mainly as a feedback: warmer air holds more water vapor, which amplifies warming started by other gases like carbon dioxide.
story:
Ryder's grandfather kept the thermostat at a temperature best described as "sweater weather in July," which meant the three of them were doing debate practice in wool socks on a Tuesday in June. Abygail had claimed the good chair by the window. Isiah lay on the rug with a legal pad on his chest, and Ryder was trying to explain, for the fourth time, why carbon dioxide mattered more than the climate skeptics on the internet said it did.

"Here's the counterargument," Isiah said, sitting up. "You're going to get this at regionals, so brace yourself. Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas. Not carbon dioxide. So warming is mostly water's fault, and CO2 is a rounding error. Go."

Ryder opened his mouth and then closed it, which Isiah found delightful. "You've been prepping this for a week," Ryder said, "and I've been prepping how to say greenhouse gases trap outgoing heat and read a CO2 graph off a projector."

"Then you lose," Isiah said, flopping back down.

Abygail pulled the graph from Ryder's folder and smoothed it on the coffee table, the one that looked like a jagged mountain range climbing a century upward. It had come from Mr. Santos-Reyes, the retired science teacher next door, along with a stack of his old textbooks and the warning that he wanted every single one back "in the condition in which they were lent, which was perfect." Ryder went to fetch the thickest one, Atmospheric Science, and found the page he'd dog-eared against Mr. Santos-Reyes's explicit rules, feeling like a criminal.

He read, and reread, and then he laughed out loud. "Okay. Okay, Isiah, you're right and also completely wrong, which is my favorite way for you to be right."

"Thank you," Isiah said graciously, from the floor.

"Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas. That part of your fake skeptic is true. But it acts mainly as a feedback." He tapped the book. "Warmer air holds more water vapor, and that amplifies the warming that other gases, like carbon dioxide, started." He looked up to see if it had landed. Abygail was already scribbling.

"So it's a follower, not a leader," she said. "CO2 nudges the temperature, and then water vapor piles on."

"Don't put it that way at regionals," Ryder said, "but yes."

Isiah sat up again, which for Isiah was practically a standing ovation. "Huh. So the skeptic's opening is actually stronger than the real answer, because the number sounds bigger, and then you have to do the work of explaining the difference." He chewed his pen. "Fine. I'm switching sides for the rest of practice. I'll run the feedback argument and you try to knock it down."

"You just lost the argument you invented," Abygail pointed out.

"I lost the argument I invented with a better argument. That's called learning. Look it up." He paused. "Actually don't, my phone's dead."

Ryder's grandfather shuffled through with two mugs of cocoa and one for himself, set them down, and said nothing, which was his version of coaching. He had grown up in a montane village where, he liked to say, you could watch weather being made over the peaks, and he considered climate science a subject for people who had never watched a cloud decide anything. But he listened from the kitchen doorway while Isiah delivered his new opening and Ryder answered, sketching the feedback loop in the air with both hands like a man describing an enormous doughnut.

Later, when the others had gone and Ryder was copying the water vapor lines onto an index card, his grandfather came in and picked up the CO2 graph. "You know what this reminds me of?" he said. "The hill behind our house, the one the goats refused to climb. Every year a little higher, and everyone acted like it had always been that steep."

"That's not really how graphs work, Grandpa."

"It's how hills work, which is the same thing." He set it down carefully, squared to the table edge, the way Mr. Santos-Reyes would want it.

Ryder looked at the card, then at the graph, then wrote one more line at the bottom in small letters: I could still be wrong about the rest. He wasn't sure that would survive regionals, where certainty was currency. He suspected it wouldn't survive his own partner, either, since Isiah would call it "surrender in writing." But the index card went into the front pocket of the folder anyway, right on top.

From the doorway, his grandfather said, "When you win, tell them about the goats."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Montana is the one US state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire a worker, under its 1987 Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act.
story:
The application had asked for her availability, her emergency contact, and whether she had ever been convicted of a felony, and Amy had answered everything honestly except the part where she wrote "flexible" and then spent an hour trying to remember what she had planned for Saturdays. She got the call on a Tuesday. Mr. Hernández wanted her at the counter of the Burger Barn on Thursday at four, one hour before the dinner rush, so she could learn the register while it was still quiet.

Thursday came and the restaurant smelled like fryer oil and floor cleaner, a smell she would later associate with the whole summer. Mr. Hernández was shorter than she had imagined on the phone, with reading glasses pushed up on his forehead, and he handed her an apron still warm from the dryer. "Ninety days probation," he said. "After that, we'll see." He said it lightly, the way people say things that mean more to the listener than the speaker, and Amy nodded as though she understood the weight of it.

She didn't, not yet. That night she told her cousin Jocelyn about the job over video call, and Jocelyn, who lived in Montana and had worked at a grocery store since March, laughed at her. "Ninety days probation. That's actually a thing here." Amy frowned at the screen. "It's a thing everywhere. That's what probation means." Jocelyn shook her head with the certainty of someone who had recently looked something up. "Not like here. In Montana, after the probationary period, the employer generally needs good cause to fire you. It's a whole law. The Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act, 1987."

"That's not real," Amy said. "Bosses can fire anyone for anything. My boss could fire me for being in a bad mood." Jocelyn's grin widened. "Mine couldn't. Not after probation. It's the one state where that's true." Amy ended the call and looked it up anyway, thumbing through the clunky state legislature website until the words appeared exactly as Jocelyn had said them. One state. She sat on her bed for a while, not because the fact changed anything for her, but because it was strange to learn that something she had assumed was fixed, like the physiology of the workday, was actually just an accident of geography. A rule could be different one state over, and she had never once wondered.

By the second week she had learned the register, the fry timers, and which regulars tipped the jar. Declan worked the grill, a year older, already past his probation, and he had a dour way of narrating everything that she found funny at first. "Patty down. Patty flipped. Patty done." On a Friday in July, though, the narration stopped being funny. A district memo had gone out about labor costs, and Mr. Hernández had started sending people home early, and Declan, who needed the hours for his car insurance, had gotten into it with him about the schedule. Voices rose behind the fry station, and then Declan threw his hat on the counter and said fine, fine, and Amy watched Mr. Hernández's face go still in a way that made her stomach drop.

Here is what she had not told anyone: she had been keeping a spiral notebook by the time clock, and in it she had begun to transcribe the schedule changes, day by day, who was sent home, who was kept, what was said. She had started it out of boredom, an English-class habit applied to fryer oil, but now the pages held three weeks of it. On Saturday she found Mr. Hernández alone in the office, counting the drawer.

"Mr. Hernández. About Declan." She laid the notebook open on the desk. He bent over it, and she pointed at Friday's entry. "You told him four o'clock, and the schedule says five. He was on time. That's why he was yelling." The office was very small and very quiet, and the drive-thru speaker crackled faintly through the wall, someone ordering without onions, and she waited while he read. "It's not my job to fix it," she said, before she could talk herself out of it. "But it wasn't his fault, and I don't want him fired over it."

Mr. Hernández straightened up and took his glasses down off his forehead. "Who told you he was getting fired?" Nobody had, exactly. She had watched a still face and done the arithmetic of it, the way you do when you're seventeen and everything feels reversible except the things that aren't. He looked at the notebook again, then at her, and closed it and slid it back across the desk. "You transcribe the whole summer?" "Most of it," she said. He didn't laugh, and he didn't explain, and she couldn't tell whether she had helped Declan or only complicated something she didn't fully see.

Monday, Declan was on the grill again, hat on, narrating patties, and nobody said a word about Friday. Jocelyn texted her that night asking how the job was, whether she'd been fired yet for being in a bad mood, and Amy typed out "not everyone lives in Montana" and then deleted it, because she still wasn't sure what the rule was here, or who held it, or how you'd ever find out until it was too late. She sent a fryer-oil emoji instead. Then she put the notebook in her backpack, zipped it, and walked to work.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: The principle is named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884.
story:
Sierra spread her chemistry notes across her grandmother's kitchen table, between the sugar bowl and a dish of peppermints that nobody ever ate. The unit test was Monday. She understood exothermic and endothermic well enough, and she could balance an equation in her sleep, but the moment the textbook began talking about equilibrium shifting, her understanding slid sideways, like something pushed. At home she had read the same paragraph four times. Here, at least, the kitchen smelled of toast and the window was open to the sound of the neighbour's wind chimes, and she could think in a different room.

The tea kettle began its low climb toward whistling. Sierra watched it, chin on her fist, and noticed that she was staring. The kettle wasn't the problem. The problem was that she could recite the rules and still not believe them. If heat was a product, then adding heat should push the reaction backward, the way extra furniture pushes people toward the walls of a room. She could verbalize it perfectly. She had verbalized it to her friend Stephan on the bus until he put in his earbuds. But reciting wasn't the same as trusting, and she wanted, before Monday, to actually trust it.

Her grandmother came in with a basket of laundry and set it on the chair. "Still working on that chemistry?"

"It's called equilibrium," Sierra said. "A reaction that goes both ways at once, and then something changes, and it, I don't know, leans." She turned her notebook sideways, as if the diagram might make more sense rotated. "It feels like metaphysics. Nothing is fixed, everything depends on what you do to it."

Her grandmother laughed and folded a towel. "That sounds like most of my life." She nodded at the tall bookcase in the hall, the one with the warped shelves. "There's an old encyclopedia in there from your grandfather's school. Chemistry under C, probably. He kept it for the smell, I think." She went out with the laundry, and Sierra, glad of any excuse, went to look.

The volume smelled like dust and pencil shavings. She carried it back to the table and found the entry, dense and small-printed, and then stopped. The principle is named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884. She read the sentence twice, then got her phone and looked him up, careful to keep the details exact, because the test would not care how interesting the man was. A portrait showed a serious man with a moustache, and for a moment the whole abstract mess in her notebook had a human face attached to it, which was somehow steadying.

Then she noticed the margins. In the entry and on the surrounding pages, someone had written in faded pencil, underlining and small notes, and the handwriting was not her grandfather's; hers she knew from birthday cards. She carried the book to the back room where her grandmother was pairing socks.

"Grandma, who wrote in this?"

Her grandmother took the volume and tilted it toward the window. "Oh," she said. "That'll be Walter. My brother." She was quiet a moment, matching a grey sock with a grey sock. "He wanted to study chemistry, back when there wasn't money for it. He bought these books secondhand from an indigent student who was selling everything he owned, a whole set for almost nothing, and Walter marked them up like he was already at university." She smiled without looking up. "He ended up running a hardware store. Good life. But he used to explain equilibrium to me at this same table when I was about your age, with the sugar bowl and everything, and I have to admit I listened the way you listen to your music."

Sierra went back to the kitchen, set the encyclopedia beside her notebook, and worked the practice problems again with the entry open in front of her, saying the name to herself at each step, the way a name can make a thing seem less like weather and more like a fact somebody discovered. When a problem asked what happens if temperature rises, she wrote her answer and, for the first time, did not feel she was guessing. Stephan texted her a question mark and a meme about failing, and she typed back, "Le Chatelier," then, "he stated it in 1884, look him up, he has a great moustache."

Later, when the kettle had cooled and her grandmother had gone to bed, Sierra sat with the book still open and copied one of Walter's pencil notes, a tiny underlined line in the margin she hadn't understood before, into her notebook so it would travel with her on Monday. Then she closed the book, and, feeling the pencil marks under her thumb like faint braille, she carried it back to the warped shelf in the hall and slid it in beside the volume that came after it.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A deductive argument is called sound only when it is valid and all of its premises are actually true, so a sound argument's conclusion must be true.
story:
The seminar room smelled of whiteboard marker and the radiator's burnt dust, and Amy had claimed the seat by the window because it let her watch the flagpole without anyone noticing where her eyes went. Ms. Guo had written a single sentence on the board, an argument about school uniforms and test scores, and sixteen of them were supposed to take it apart. Amy wanted, more than she wanted anything else that morning, to be the one who took it apart first, cleanly, before Callie could.

Callie sat across the table with her laptop open, though she never typed anything; she just liked the barrier of it. Last spring, at the regional debate final, Callie had beaten Amy with an argument about later school start times, and Amy had lost not because her rebuttals were weak but because she had answered the wrong thing. She had attacked the shape of Callie's case when its weakness lay elsewhere, somewhere she couldn't name at the time, and the loss had become a kind of leitmotif in her head, returning whenever she opened her notes to a blank page.

"The argument's valid," Alexia was saying, tapping the board with the cap of her pen. "If uniforms raise scores, and the school adopts uniforms, then scores rise. That follows. You can't argue with the structure."

Amy wrote the three lines in her notebook, bracketed them, and stared at the middle one. If uniforms raise scores. Something about it prickled at her, the way a loose thread prickles before you find it. She remembered Callie in the final, calm and fluent, and she remembered the judge afterward saying the case "held together." Held together. Like a suture, she thought; the stitches could be perfect and the wound still infected. The reasoning could be flawless and carry something false inside it.

"I think it's valid but not sound," Amy said, before she could decide whether she wanted to say it. The word came out and she let it stand. "Sound only counts when it's valid and the premises are all actually true. So if the conclusion has to be true, the whole thing has to be sound. That first premise, that uniforms raise scores, is just false. There was that study Ms. Guo showed us last month, the one that found no effect."

The room went quiet in the way it does when someone has moved the furniture. Callie looked up from her laptop screen, and Amy saw her expression shift, not to anger but to recognition, the look of someone finding a name for a thing she had sensed herself. "That's what you should have said in the final," Callie said. "My start-times case rested on a attendance figure I got from one district. One. You kept attacking my logic instead."

Ms. Guo, who had been leaning against the filing cabinet with her arms folded, pushed off and walked to the board. "So which matters more," she asked the room, not Amy, "a valid argument or a true premise?" Alexia argued for validity, trenchant as always: structure was checkable, transferable, teachable, while truth was messy and expensive to verify. Callie argued, unexpectedly, for truth: an argument that proves nothing true is a beautiful machine with no product. Amy listened with her pen still and realized she no longer wanted to win this; she wanted to hold both claims at once, the way you hold two handles of the same heavy bag.

The window had fogged at the corner where her breath reached it, and the flag outside hung limp, then lifted, then hung again. Amy thought of her father, who fixed washing machines and refused to argue at dinner because, he said, most arguments are two people defending premises nobody checked. She had thought that was resignation when she was twelve. Now it sounded closer to a method.

"I'd say this," Amy offered, when the pause found her. "Validity tells you what follows if the premises are true. Soundness is the whole promise, structure plus fact, and only the whole promise guarantees the conclusion." Then she hesitated, because something in her wasn't finished. "But I still can't always tell when a premise is false. Half the time I can't even tell which of my own I've never checked." She looked at Callie, who was smiling faintly, a little sadly, at the board.

Ms. Guo erased the middle line, wrote a question mark in its place, and set the marker down on the rail. "For Thursday," she said, "bring one premise you believe and haven't tested. One will be enough."

"Mine's about later start times," Callie said, and closed her laptop.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: On 28 March 1979, the UK government of James Callaghan lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote, 311 to 310, forcing a general election.
story:
Layla spread her notes across the library table like evidence at a trial nobody was attending. On the left page, a diagram of how Britain chose and could dismiss a prime minister; on the right, the same for an American president. The two systems stared at each other across the spine of her open notebook, and she had written, in the margin, "who exactly holds the knife?"

"You're doing the Schneider assignment?" Alexanne dropped into the chair opposite, unwrapping a granola bar despite the sign. "He gave me a C on my last one. He said I described things instead of arguing."

"I'm trying to argue. The problem is I don't know what I think yet." Layla turned the notebook so Alexanne could see. "In a parliamentary system the head of government isn't elected separately. The party wins seats, the party picks the leader, and if the party turns on him, or if parliament turns on the party, he's out. In the presidential system you elect the president directly, more or less, and short of death or impeachment he serves his term. So the question is whether it's better to be removable or stable."

"You sound like a textbook." Alexanne crumpled the wrapper. "Also you said him. Could be a her."

"Could be." Layla had not thought of that, and it bothered her, the way assumptions surfaced only when someone pointed at them.

She went back to the shelves. Mr. Schneider, at the reference desk, had suggested the politics section with the ascetic efficiency of a man who believed every question had a shelf and every shelf had an answer. The fluorescent lights made the carpet's pattern undulate faintly if she let her eyes blur, and she did this without meaning to, walking the aisle, until a fat blue book on British politics stopped her. She carried it to the window seat where the light was honest.

The chapter on the 1970s was dry until it wasn't. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, and felt something shift in her chest like a door swinging on a stuck hinge. On 28 March 1979, the government of James Callaghan lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote, 311 to 310, and was forced into a general election. One vote. A government, gone. She checked the numbers again, wanting them to be wrong or to mean less, and they refused.

She carried the book back to the table at speed. "Alexanne. One vote. In 1979 one vote brought down the entire British government."

"One what now?"

"A vote of no confidence, it's called. Parliament votes on whether it still backs the government, and if the government loses, there has to be an election." Layla sat down too hard and the table rattled. "It was 311 to 310. March 28th. Callaghan. One man, one abstention, whatever it was, and the whole thing came down."

Alexanne looked at her with the wary respect of someone watching a friend take on a new religion. "Okay. And you're telling me this because?"

"Because we sat through that assembly where they told us our votes don't matter, that one vote never changes anything. And here's a whole government, dissolved over one." She pulled the notebook toward her and started writing, fast. "That's my argument. In a parliamentary system, numbers this thin can actually decide something. Removal isn't a constitutional crisis, it's a Tuesday. In the presidential system, if the legislature hates the president, they still have to wait, unless they can impeach, which almost never works. Power and accountability sit in separate rooms."
