"Louis-Felix would say the separate rooms are the point," Alexanne said. "That you don't want a government collapsing every time somebody sneezes."

Layla stopped writing. Louis-Felix had argued exactly that in class on Tuesday, smoothly, the way he argued everything, and she had resented it and then quietly half-agreed with it. "Stability is real," she admitted. "A country that can shed its government overnight can also be jerked around by whoever holds that one vote. It cuts both ways." She underlined the numbers. "But I'd rather live somewhere the powerful can actually be made to answer, even messily, than somewhere the only real firing is an election years away. I think that's my position. I think."

"You think you think?"

"I'm sure about the fact. I'm less sure about what follows from it." She said it plainly, because it was true, and because pretending otherwise would make the whole paper a kind of parasitism, her argument feeding on a number she hadn't earned the right to stretch.

Alexanne checked the time and started gathering her things. "Tell Schneider about the one vote. Lead with it. He likes being startled."

Layla sat with the blue book a while longer after Alexanne left, copying the date onto an index card, then the two numbers, then the name. Around her the afternoon patrons came and went, and somewhere near the printers a machine hummed and fell silent. She squared the card against the notebook's edge, and slid it into her pocket.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate.
story:
The season ended on a Tuesday in October, with a 2-1 loss in the park's east field, and by Saturday the whole team had been cajoled into showing up at the same picnic shelter for the end-of-season party. Tyler's mother had volunteered him to carry the coolers, so he arrived first, before the streamers went up, when the shelter was still just a gray roof on posts and the soccer goals stood empty in the distance like frames for pictures nobody had taken yet. He set the coolers down and stood there longer than he needed to.

Tyler was a junior, which meant this party was a rehearsal. Next year he would be a senior, and next year's party would be his. But for Phillip and Emile, who had started on this team together at fourteen and now wore the armbands, this was the real thing, and Tyler could already see it in how they moved through the shelter, slower than usual, touching the picnic tables like they were counting them.

Ms. Lim, who coached the team and lived two streets from the park, brought a sheet cake with the league standings written in icing. Third place. Nobody pretended that was what they'd wanted, but everybody ate it anyway, and for an hour the party was just a party: Emile doing his impression of the referee from the semifinal, Phillip trying to get the younger players to attempt his throw-in, which none of them could.

Then the light started going amber over the trees, and the mood shifted the way it does at the end of things. Phillip climbed onto a table and said he had a speech, and it was terrible, half jokes and half not, and at the end of it he said, "Fourteen years I've played with some of you. That's most of my life." He got down fast, before his face could catch up with what he'd said.

Emile was quieter. He sat on the bench beside Tyler with his plate balanced on his knees and said he'd been reading something for a psychology paper, about how groups develop. "Everyone knows the stages," he said. "Forming, storming, norming, performing. But in 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate." He poked at his cake. "I kept thinking it was the saddest word for it. Adjourning. Like we're a meeting."

Tyler said he didn't think it was sad. He said adjourning was what a court did when it planned to come back, and he wasn't sure that was the right way to think about it either, because this team would never reconvene, not with these exact people. Ms. Lim, folding chairs nearby, said nothing, only looked over once, and Tyler lowered his voice, aware that the coach had opinions about treating sports like a class.

"It's like the team's an oligarchy," Phillip said, dropping onto the bench across from them. "Seniors rule, then they're gone, and it's just the next ones." He meant it as a joke, but the three of them sat with it. Tyler found himself arguing the other side without quite deciding to: the team wasn't ruled so much as passed along, the same drills, the same shelter, the same cake with the standings on it, and maybe that was the difference between a group that adjourned and one that just changed its members. Though, he admitted, he couldn't tell which one this was. He was honest about that. He didn't know whether Phillip and Emile were leaving the team or whether the team was leaving them.

Someone turned on the shelter's one weak bulb, and moths began circling it, and someone's little brother was already untying one of the streamers. Ms. Lim said they had the field booked until nine if anyone wanted a last kickaround, no drills, just playing, and Phillip stood up first and jogged out toward the goals in his sneakers, and Emile followed, and Tyler went after them with the cake still sweet in his mouth. Emile stopped at the halfway line and turned around once to look back at the lit shelter, the streamers sagging, the folding chairs stacked, and then Phillip shouted his name from the box, and Emile ran on.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: The Heckscher-Ohlin model, named after Swedish economists Eli Heckscher and Bertil Ohlin, explains comparative advantage by differences in countries' supplies of land, labor and capital.
story:
Peyton was supposed to be stocking cans of chickpeas, but the economics study guide was propped between the cans and a tower of tomato paste, and she was muttering at it. The store was dead for a Tuesday, the lights buzzing above aisle four, and Mr. Hussain, the manager, had told her twice that reading on shift was a privilege, not a right, delivered with the exact tone of a man quoting his own employee handbook.

"Quiz me," she said when Kristopher appeared at the end of the aisle, allegedly shopping for his mother, realistically hiding from a Saturday shift at the hardware store.

"Fine. Why do two countries both gain from trading, even when one of them is better at everything?"

"Comparative advantage." She shelved a can with a flourish. "You don't compare how good each country is at making a thing. You compare what each country gives up to make it. So even the country that's worse at both things should do the one it's less bad at, and trade for the rest. Both sides gain. It's practically axiomatic."

"That's the vocab word, yeah. But Mr. Delgado wants the why underneath it. Why do the advantages even exist?"

This was where the study guide got smudgy. Peyton had read the paragraph four times on the bus, and it kept sliding off her brain like oil off a nonstick pan. She said as much, and Kristopher picked up a chickpea can, turned it over as though the answer might be printed under the ingredients.

Camden arrived carrying a basket with one lemon in it, which was a Camden kind of basket. "I heard econ from two aisles away. It has a sound, you know. Like a dying radiator."

"Quiz her on the why," Kristopher said.

"On the why of what?"

"Why countries have comparative advantage in the first place."

Camden set the lemon on the shelf between the chickpeas, a tiny yellow intruder, and Peyton stared at it and then, oddly, at the whole aisle. Bags of rice from one country. Olive oil from another. A whole wall of the world sorted into categories, and her name tag pinned above it.

"Okay, hang on," she said. "Take a country with a huge amount of farmland. Land everywhere, right? So growing grain costs it, like, nothing. Meanwhile some other country has factories everywhere, tons of capital, hardly any fields. The first country exports grain. The second exports electronics. They trade, both gain, because of what each one has a lot of." She paused. "There was a name for this. Two Swedish guys."

"Heckscher and Ohlin," said Mr. Hussain, from behind them, holding a clipboard.

Three heads turned. "How do you know that?" Peyton asked.

"I did not spend four years in a graduate economics program to run a grocery store," Mr. Hussain said, "and yet here we are." He picked up Camden's lemon, looked at it with faint disapproval, and set it back down. "Also, you are being paid to face the labels outward, Peyton, not inward. The label faces the customer."

"The Heckscher-Ohlin model," Peyton said slowly, watching him. "Named after Swedish economists Eli Heckscher and Bertil Ohlin. It explains comparative advantage by differences in countries' supplies of land, labor and capital. Land, labor, capital. That's the whole why."

"That is the whole why," Mr. Hussain agreed. "Though you have now learned it by shoplifting it from the air, which I cannot put on your performance review."

The twist came at the register ten minutes later, when a woman Peyton had never seen before unloaded a cart of pasta and asked, idly, why the grain was from overseas when they grew wheat two counties over. Peyton opened her mouth to launch into comparative advantage, absolute advantage, the entire unit, and Camden, bagging groceries with terrible speed, caught her eye and shook his head slightly. So Peyton only said, "Probably price," and scanned the pasta, and the woman left satisfied.

"You knew the whole answer," Camden said afterward, "and you didn't use it."

"It wasn't the question she was really asking. She was asking why her local farm lost, and no model answers that." Peyton straightened the receipt paper. "That's the part the study guide doesn't cover. The model says both countries gain. It doesn't say everybody in both countries gains. I don't actually know what I think about that yet."

"Arbitration," Kristopher offered, appearing with a candy bar he had no intention of paying for. "You could decide the losers get compensated. Someone would have to decide."

"That's between the countries, not the farmers." She took the candy bar out of his hand and scanned it, adding it to her own total, which had the effect of enfranchising his appetite at her expense. He grinned and paid her back in quarters, counting them out onto the belt like a tiny ransom.

The store emptied toward evening. Peyton faced the labels outward, aisle by aisle, and found herself reading them, country of origin after country of origin, a passport stamp on every can. Mr. Hussain passed with his clipboard and paused at the lemon, still sitting among the chickpeas.

"Your friend has left a citrus in the legumes," he said. "Some trade, in my opinion, benefits no one."

Peyton laughed, picked it up, and rang it through on Camden's abandoned tab.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Mexico's Day of the Dead is traditionally celebrated on November 1 and 2, when families build ofrendas, or home altars, with photos and the favorite foods and drinks of relatives who have died.
story:
The nurse came at 11:40 on the first of November and drew the curtain around the bed in the corner, and after that the room was not Hannah's grandmother's room anymore, only a room. Her father made calls in the hallway, his voice flattening the way it did when he spoke to his own mother long distance. Hannah sat with her backpack between her knees, the backpack she had brought for three days of sitting, and inside it the marigolds she had never gotten to put in the water pitcher.

Her mother arrived before dawn and knelt in front of Hannah, holding her wrists. "We need you to do something," she said. "Abuela's sister is coming tonight, and we're building the ofrenda. You know what that is?"

"The altar," Hannah said. "Day of the Dead. November first and second." She had learned it in Ms. Li's class two weeks ago, sitting beside Makai, who had drawn a skull in the margin of his notes and written Hannah's name under it as a joke she hadn't found funny at the time.

"Her sister says we put out photos, and her favorite foods, her favorite drinks. Whatever she loved. But Hannah, I don't know what my mother loved anymore. I know what she cooked for everyone else. Flan, café de olla. When did I last see her eat something just for herself?"

"The pan dulce," Hannah said. "The pink one with the sugar crust. She'd buy it and hide it from us so it wouldn't be gone by Sunday."

Her mother closed her eyes for a second. "Can you find it? The panadería on Division closes at two, and Tía Rosa lands at eight. It has to be on the altar by tonight, or it isn't Day of the Dead anymore, it's just a table."

Hannah texted Makai from the hospital elevator, and by the time she reached the lobby Emelia had already replied too, both of them offering to drive, neither asking what had happened because the words "my grandma died an hour ago" at the top of the thread made asking unnecessary. Emelia's car smelled like the french fries she ate on the way home from debate, and she let Hannah hold the aux cord without playing anything, which Hannah understood as a form of kindness.

At school, in Ms. Li's class, they had argued about rituals that morning, or the morning of some day that now seemed to belong to a different, intact world. Makai had called tradition a kind of oligarchy, a rule handed down by the dead who couldn't be voted out, and Emelia had said that was exactly backwards, that rituals were the only vote the dead got. Hannah had said nothing, because her grandmother was dying and every position on the subject felt like trespass. Now, watching Emelia's wipers push rain sideways, she thought that both of them were describing the same thing from two sides, and that her own answer was going to have to be made with her hands, tonight, out of marigolds and bread.

The panadería had one concha left with the pink crust, set apart from the rest as if reserved. The cashier, an older man, wrapped it slowly and then added, without being asked, a second one with a yellow crust, no charge. "For the altar," he said. "You have the photos? And something to drink? They get thirsty, the dead, on the long way back." Hannah had read the last part somewhere, or maybe he had just made it up, and she didn't ask which, because either way he was handing it to her like something true.

At the house her mother and father were still arguing over the photo, the formal one from the fifties with the florid gold frame, where her grandmother looked like a stranger who happened to share her jaw, against the Polaroid from the lake where she was laughing so hard her eyes were closed. Hannah set the bread in the center before they decided, and then the photograph they had been fighting over didn't seem to matter as much, because the whole table rearranged itself around what the bread said about who she had been. Her father went quiet. He put the Polaroid on the left, the gold frame empty behind it.

Tía Rosa arrived at eight with a suitcase and cempasúchil petals in a plastic bag, damp from some other city. She touched the concha's sugar crust with one finger and said, "This was hers," and sat down in the nearest chair and wept in a way that made Hannah's father cross the room. Later there would be a fight, Hannah knew, about the frame and the flowers and all the things grief tries to extenuate, but for now Tía Rosa asked for coffee, two cups, one for herself, and her father poured it without a word.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Adolphe Thiers's History of the French Revolution, published from 1823 to 1827, praised moderate leaders such as Mirabeau and Lafayette and condemned radicals such as Robespierre.
story:
Savannah had chosen the war memorial because it was the only place in town where nobody asked her anything. The monument sat on a rise behind the library, a granite soldier staring west, its base carved with names from two wars, and on Saturday mornings the benches around it belonged to pigeons and to her. She spread her notes across the cold stone: three library books, a photocopied article, and the assignment sheet from Ms. Wiśniewski, which asked for a historiographical essay, an account not of the French Revolution itself but of how its meaning had been fought over since 1800.

The problem was that she couldn't find the argument. She had read that early historians treated the Revolution as a tragedy of excess, that later ones recuperated its radical phase as a necessary birth pangs of democracy, and that the pendulum had swung again after the Soviet archives opened, when terror lost its romantic defenders. But a list of swings wasn't a thesis. Ms. Wiśniewski had written one comment in red pen on her draft outline: "Who is doing the swinging, and why does it matter?" Savannah had no answer, only a stack of index cards she kept reshuffling like a losing hand.

Shane arrived at eleven, hood up, carrying two coffees and his phone in his fist. He'd been to Paris in the spring with his mother, and Ms. Wiśniewski had suggested, with what Savannah found a slightly sardonic lift of the eyebrow, that he might have seen something relevant. He sat down on the memorial steps without ceremony, among the carved names of the dead.

"Okay," he said. "So I texted you about the statue. There's this guy, Thiers, near where we stayed. Big bronze figure, and I only stopped because Mom made me take a picture of every old man on a pedestal. I read the plaque to be polite." He turned the phone toward her. "Adolphe Thiers. And the plaque said he was a historian and a statesman, which I thought was a weird order, so I looked him up on the walk back to the hotel."

Savannah scrolled through his photos. There he was, long coat, one hand in the plaster, standing above Parisian rooftops.

"So here's the thing," Shane said. "Before he ran France, he wrote its history. The History of the French Revolution, came out from 1823 to 1827. And he praised Mirabeau and Lafayette and condemned Robespierre." He said it flatly, the way he'd memorized it off the screen. "Moderates good, radical bad. That's the whole book, basically."

Savannah's pen stopped. In her notes Thiers had been a paragraph, a name attached to the phrase "bourgeois liberal narrative," and she had skimmed past him toward Marxists and revisionists because the textbook made him sound like a warm-up act. But he had written his history in the 1820s, while the men he was judging were close enough to touch, while people who had wept at Robespierre's fall were still alive to buy the volumes. A man who would later crush the Paris Commune had already decided, in advance, which revolution deserved to survive. She wrote fast, filling a card, then another, then flipping the first card over because she'd run out of room.

"So use him," Shane said, watching her write. He sounded faintly wounded, as if he'd handed her a gift and she'd started repairing it. "He's your swinging."

"Maybe." She looked up at the granite soldier above them, at the name of a boy from her street who had died at nineteen, younger than she was, in a war that had once been called the war to end war and was now called World War One, its meaning already rewritten twice before her grandmother was born. "That's what I can't figure out. If Thiers was choosing his heroes in 1823, and everybody after him was choosing theirs, then either everyone was dishonest or nobody was. And if nobody was, then what is the essay even about?"

They argued about it through one coffee and into the second. Shane thought it was simple, that the truth accumulated like sediment, each generation adding a layer. Savannah thought it was more like the dialectic Ms. Wiśniewski kept naming in class, each account contradicting the last and forcing something harder out of the collision. But when she tried to say which one she believed, she found herself hedging, and she was honest enough with Shane, and with herself, to say so out loud. "I think the historians are reacting to each other, not just to the Revolution," she said. "But I can't prove they're not reacting to their own present. Maybe both. I don't know how to hold both in one thesis sentence."

Shane shrugged and stood, collecting the empty cups, pointing out that the wind was coming up and the pigeons were reclaiming the bench. "Write the both," he said. "It's more interesting than the sediment thing anyway." He crumpled the cups into the bin by the memorial gate and turned up the hill toward home.

Savannah stayed a while longer. The light had moved, and the granite soldier's shadow now lay across the lowest line of carved names, covering some and not others as the afternoon wore on. She copied Thiers into her notebook with the dates exactly as Shane had said them, underlined the names Mirabeau and Lafayette and Robespierre, and then wrote beneath, in smaller letters, the question she would open the essay with and could not yet answer. She gathered her cards, squared them against the bench, and walked down past the library with the wind pulling the pages apart in her hand, holding them shut with her thumb.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Consent to sexual activity must be freely given and can be withdrawn at any time, including after activity has already started.
story:
Rose had chosen the dentist's waiting room because it was the only place where her mother could not follow her with questions, and because the appointment gave the whole thing an alibi. Maina and Kaitlin sat on either side of her, the three of them wedged between a rack of dog-eared magazines and a television muted to a weather forecast, and on Rose's lap lay the folder she had been assembling for two weeks: consent, contraception, where to get tested, everything she was supposed to teach on Saturday to the younger girls at the community centre.

"Start from the top," Maina said, though she kept her voice low, aware of the older man two chairs down and the receptionist behind her glass. "You're the counselor, I'm the one who came in."

Rose set the folder on her knees and straightened it. "Okay. Hi. Welcome to the clinic. What can I do for you today?"

"I want to know about the pill," Maina said, dropping her voice further, "but my boyfriend says if I get it he'll tell everyone I'm easy."

Kaitlin made a small noise of disgust. Rose felt her mouth go dry. She had an answer written in the folder, something about confidentiality, about nobody being told anything without permission, but the sentences she had copied from the health service website suddenly seemed to belong to someone else, someone calmer, someone who had not once stood in a hallway while a boy laughed about a girl in their grade.

"Nobody at the clinic tells anyone," she said. "It's confidential. Not your boyfriend, not your parents."

"Even if I'm underage?"

Rose checked the folder. "There are rules about that, but mostly yes."

Then Kaitlin leaned forward, chin in her hand, wearing the smile she used when she had already won an argument. "Okay, but here's my question. Say somebody said yes at the start. They wanted to. Then halfway through they change their mind. That's allowed? Saying yes earlier doesn't lock you in?"

Rose opened her mouth to preempt her, to say something smooth about communication, and then realized she did not actually know. She had read the page on consent three times. She had highlighted a sentence in yellow. And still, faced with Kaitlin's flat stare, she could not remember whether it had said yes means yes until you say no, or something harder than that.

"Honestly," she said, "I think I'm about to get it wrong, so give me a second."

Maina laughed, briefly, and the man two chairs down glanced over. Rose turned the folder pages, past the diagrams of contraception she had been embarrassed to photocopy, until she found the highlighted line. She read it once to herself, then again, and something in her chest loosened.

"It has to be freely given," she said. "And you can take it back at any time. Even after it's already started. Yes at the beginning isn't a contract."

"You looked that up," Kaitlin said.

"I'm looking it up now. That counts." Rose closed the folder on her thumb to hold the page. "Saturday, if someone asks me that, I'll say exactly this. Freely given, and you can withdraw it whenever, even mid-activity. If the other person keeps going, that's not a misunderstanding anymore."

Kaitlin was quiet for a moment, and Rose understood, the way you understand a whole phylum of creatures by examining one specimen, that the question had not been hypothetical for her either, or for someone Kaitlin knew. Neither of them said so. The muted television cycled from weather to weather.

"Rose Martel?" The hygienist stood at the little door with a clipboard, and Rose gathered her folder and followed, and that should have been the end of it.

She was in the chair for twenty minutes with a sealant on a back molar, and when she came out with one numb cheek, Ms. Petrov was at the desk and the waiting room had emptied except for one girl, maybe fourteen, sitting very straight with her hands folded, wearing a school uniform from a school Rose did not recognize. Maina and Kaitlin had moved to the window and were pretending to be fascinated by parking meters.

Ms. Petrov caught Rose's eye on her way past. "Your friends are lively," she said, not unkindly. "That was quite the tutorial on, what was it, clinic services?" Rose felt her face heat, but Ms. Petrov only added, "The sink in three is dripping again, tell your mother," and disappeared behind the door, which was either discretion or indifference, and Rose found she did not need to know which.

The girl in the uniform was still watching her. When Rose and her friends collected their bags, the girl stood too, and at the doorway, in the cold strip of light between the waiting room and the street, she spoke so quietly that only Rose caught it.

"Is it really true nobody gets told? At that clinic you said."

Rose thought about her folder, about Saturday, about how little she knew and how much of it she had gotten wrong in her own kitchen before she got it right in a dentist's chair. Being altruistic was easy to write in a personal statement; standing in a doorway with a fourteen-year-old waiting on an answer was something else.

"You can call and ask them anything first, without giving your name," Rose said, and dug a card out of the folder, the one with the clinic's hours on it, and held it out. "That's what I did."

The girl took the card with both hands, the way you take something you intend to keep.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: The AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio's Selected Works section asks for 5 artworks and counts for 40 percent of the score.
story:
The art building at Camp Wenlock smelled of cedar shavings and turpentine, and Maelie had claimed the corner easel by the window on the first day, before anyone else understood how the afternoon light moved across it. Now, twelve days in, she had nine pieces taped to the wall behind her, all of them rivers: the river behind her grandmother's house, the river in a photograph Liliane had taken of her own grandfather's hands, the river Maelie had imagined under the highway near school, silted and gray. The assignment was to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme, with an artist's statement, and she had decided, with a confidence she did not entirely feel, that her theme was water that carries things away.

"So what's number ten?" Liliane asked, kneeling on the floor with a jar of brushes. She had been sorting them for twenty minutes, which was Liliane's way of staying near someone without having to ask if they wanted company.

"I don't know yet. Something about flooding, maybe. Or the delta." Maelie turned a pencil over in her fingers. "The alluvial fan. Where the river drops everything it carried."

"That's the one from yesterday, though. The mud one."

"It's related. It's not the same."

Liliane held up two brushes, compared them, put both back. "It's kind of the same."

In the back room, Montana was arguing with the camp's only scanner, which had begun eating the edges of anything fed into it. Montana wanted digital images of everything before Friday, because Montana was applying to programs that required slides, and her whole body had the strained posture of someone who had realized, midsummer, that time was short. Maelie had offered her window easel for the scanning light, and Montana had said, "You don't have to," and then set up beside her anyway.

The trouble was not the tenth piece. The trouble was that Ms. Buchanan had pinned a photocopied page to the corkboard by the door, and Maelie had read it three times that morning while pretending to rinse her brushes. It concerned the AP portfolio, the one Maelie had assumed she would submit in the spring, the one her school offered as a single course with a single score. The page said the Selected Works section asked for five artworks and counted for forty percent of that score. Five. Out of everything she might make between now and May, five pieces would carry nearly half the weight, and the rest, the sustained investigation, would carry the rest. She had assumed it would be the opposite, that the big body of work would matter most. She stood at the sink a long time, water running over her hands, doing the arithmetic again as though the numbers might rearrange themselves.

"Is that true?" she asked Montana that afternoon, while they waited for the scanner to think. "The five pieces thing. Forty percent."

"Yeah." Montana squared a drawing against the glass. "Five strongest. They want your best five, and those five are almost half your score. My cousin did it. She picked wrong, she thinks. She picked the ones her teacher liked instead of the ones she liked."

"What happened?"

"She got a three. She won't talk about it." The scanner groaned and began its slow pass.

Maelie looked at her wall of rivers. The mud piece was good, she knew it was good, but it was quiet; it did not announce itself the way the flood piece did, all that panicked white water. Her mother's maxim came back to her, the one about squeaky wheels and grease, and she had always disliked it, and yet here she was, suspecting that the graders, whoever they were, would hear the loud pieces and skim past the delta. And there was the other voice in her, Liliane's, or maybe her grandmother's, which said that the quiet work was the real work, that anything you make only to be chosen has already been given away. She could not make both voices into one. She could only notice that they disagreed, and keep painting anyway, and let the choosing come later, badly or well.

On Thursday she made the tenth piece, small, a river gone thin in August, stones showing through like vertebrae. When it was dry she hung it between the flood and the mud, low on the wall where the light was worst, and stepped back. Liliane came over with two mugs of the terrible camp coffee and gave her one without being asked.

"Number ten," Maelie said.

Liliane studied the wall for a while. "It's the best one," she said finally.

"It's the smallest."

"I know." Liliane drank her coffee and made a face at it. "I still think so."

Maelie sat down on the stool and pulled out a notebook and wrote, at the top of a clean page, "Which five," and beneath it, nothing yet. Outside, the actual river, the one the camp was built around, moved past in the late light, carrying whatever it carried.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: In common-law jurisdictions, including most of the US, a contract made by a minor is generally voidable by the minor, with exceptions such as contracts for necessities.
story:
The cursor blinked at the top of a page titled "Contracts and Minors: An Overview," and Matthew read the first sentence twice before it settled into him. Three weeks ago he had stood at the front desk of Riverside Fitness with a pen in his hand and a seventeen-year-old's signature withheld, because the girl behind the counter had slid the form back across the desk and said his mother needed to sign it. Tonight, eighteen and home alone with his laptop open on the kitchen table, he wanted to know whether she had been right, and whether it mattered that he wasn't seventeen anymore.

He typed "why does gym need parent signature for 17 year old" into the search bar and watched the results load. The first three were forum posts from parents complaining about liability waivers. The fourth was from a legal aid site, plainly written, and it said something that stopped him: in common-law jurisdictions, including most of the United States, a contract made by a minor is generally voidable by the minor. He sat back. Voidable. He said the word out loud to the empty kitchen, and it had a strange weight, like a door that could be closed after you had already walked through it.

His phone buzzed against the table. It was Trace, asking if Matthew had finished the physics problem set, but Matthew typed back something else first. "Did you know you can basically back out of a contract if you're underage?" A long pause, then three dots, then: "are you suing the gym or what." Matthew laughed, a short sound in the quiet room, and explained about the counter girl and the form, the small print he had read while his mother was still in the parking lot.

"You're making this up," Trace wrote. "I signed a phone contract when I was sixteen."

"Voidable by the minor," Matthew typed. "That's the phrase. Not void, voidable. You could have backed out."

"Nobody backed me out of anything. I still owe forty a month."

The exceptions were next. The site listed them in a gray box: contracts for necessities were treated differently. Food, lodging, medical care. Matthew chewed the inside of his cheek and thought about it. A phone plan, a gym membership, a car, a year of streaming services, all of it entered into by teenagers with jobs and debit cards, and all of it apparently resting on a rule nobody had told them. It didn't thrill him the way a loophole would have; it unsettled him instead, the way discovering that the ground you had walked on was thinner than you thought. He kept reading anyway. The subject had begun to enthrall him, the old language of assent and consideration, words that sounded like they belonged to some taciturn old profession that spoke only in binding sentences.

He opened a second tab and found the Riverside Fitness membership agreement, still hosted on their site, still eleven pages long. He scrolled to the section on liability and read the clauses about injury and assumption of risk. His own signature was on page nine, his mother's cramped initials below it. He remembered how she had read only the payment section and signed the rest without slowing down, saying the whole thing was standard. At the time he had thought she was careless. Now he wondered whether she had simply learned what the law already knew, that her son's promise at seventeen had been a soft thing, cancellable, and that her signature had been the hard one.

The kitchen light hummed overhead. Down the hall, the floor creaked where the house settled, and Mr. Boateng's voice drifted faintly through the shared wall, talking to someone on his own phone about a fence contractor and a deposit. Matthew typed a message to Olivia, who wanted to be a paralegal and said so at every opportunity. "Question. If a minor signs a gym contract, can the gym enforce it?" Her reply came fast, with a link to the same legal aid site he had already read. "Mostly no," she added. "That's why gyms want the parent. The parent can't void it." Matthew read that twice. It was the piece he had been circling without naming it. The gym hadn't wanted his mother's signature to be polite. They had wanted someone on the hook who could not walk away.

Still, the uneasiness didn't fully resolve itself. He scrolled back to the exceptions and found the borders of the rule blurrier than the rule itself. Necessities were one thing, but a judge deciding what counted seemed like another thing entirely, and the site said nothing about which side a gym membership fell on in his state, or whether a phone plan was a necessity for a boy who needed it for work. Trace had sent another message, a joke about hiring Matthew as his lawyer, fee payable in a voidable contract. Matthew smiled at it and didn't answer right away. He looked at his own signature on page nine, at his mother's initials, at the small line at the bottom that said this agreement constituted the entire understanding between the parties. Somewhere in that pile of clauses, he thought, was the difference between what people agreed to and what people were bound to, and he had spent one evening learning that the difference was real without learning where it ended.

He copied the link to the legal aid page and pasted it into his chat with Trace, then typed one more line before closing the laptop.

"Read it before you sign anything else."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In a standard repayment mortgage, early monthly payments go mostly toward interest, and later payments go mostly toward paying down the amount borrowed.
story:
Xavier had come to his grandmother's house that Saturday to help clear the garage, and instead he had spent an hour listening to his cousin cry at the kitchen table. She was twenty-six, older than him by the kind of gap that had once seemed enormous and now seemed like nothing. Between the crying she kept saying the same phrase, "five years of payments," as though repeating it would make it mean something different. Her statement from the bank lay open on the table, and when she pushed it toward him, Xavier read the number twice before he understood what he was looking at.

"It's a standard repayment mortgage," she said. "That's what the man called it. I pay every month, I've never missed one, and look how little I still owe."

Xavier looked. Five years of monthly payments had barely reduced the amount she'd borrowed. The early payments, she said she'd found out from a friend at work, went mostly toward interest, and only the later ones would go mostly toward paying down the loan itself. She had assumed the reverse, that every payment carved a neat equal slice off the debt. She had been building equity the way a person fills a bathtub with a thimble.

"You're eighteen," she said, wiping her face with the heel of her hand. "You haven't even started. Don't do what I did. Don't just sign things."

Xavier didn't point out that she had signed for a house, which was more than most people their family had ever signed for. His grandmother's house, the one they were sitting in, had been bought outright in 1971 with money his grandfather had saved working nights at the plant, before Xavier's father was born. There had been no deposit, no down payment, no interest, only cash and a handshake with a man whose name nobody remembered now. The house sat on its quarter acre like a tectonic fact, something the whole family arranged itself around, its stability assumed so completely it was never discussed.

His father rented. He had rented for twenty years, apartments then duplexes then the small house on Cochrane Street, handing over a deposit on each one, that first month's rent plus a sum held against damage, returned when they left if the walls were clean. Xavier had watched him vacuum the carpets of an empty apartment at midnight once, at fourteen, so the landlord couldn't keep four hundred dollars, and his father had said, "It's not about the money, it's about them finding a reason." Xavier had thought about that phrase for years, turning it over, and he still wasn't sure what it meant to owe someone nothing and have them look anyway.

For a while he had pathologized it, decided his father was careless with money, insolvency waiting in the shape of a man, and he'd said as much to his friend Adrien senior year, who had laughed at him. "Your dad raised you on a renter's salary," Adrien said. "Half the people pathologizing him couldn't do it." Adrien's parents owned; there was a stillness in Adrien about money, an absence of flinching, that Xavier had noticed the way you notice someone doesn't limp.

Now the cousin was talking about selling. She wanted out from under the loan, wanted to rent again, something smaller, and Xavier found himself arguing before he'd decided to. "If you sell now," he said, "you've paid five years of mostly interest and you keep almost none of it. If you stay, the later payments actually reduce what you owe. That's what you said." She stared at him. "That's the trap," she said. "It's a trap that only works if you never leave." Xavier said maybe that was just what a house was, and she said he sounded like their grandfather, and neither of them decided whether that was a compliment.

His grandmother came in from the garden with tomatoes in a bowl and set them down between the bank statement and the cousin's car keys. She didn't ask. She poured three glasses of the iced tea she'd been making since before either of them existed and said the garage could wait one more Saturday. The cousin reached for her glass, and Xavier watched her hand steady itself around it, and outside the screen door the yard went on being green and owned and quiet. "Ten more years," she said, mostly to the table. "Ten more years and it turns over, and the payments start landing somewhere." Xavier picked up a tomato and turned it over, looking for the soft side.
